insights.summary: 全国工商联发布2026中国民营企业500强榜单，500强营收总额44.93万亿元，同比增长4.35%。车企中比亚迪、吉利跻身前十，比亚迪以8039.6亿元营收位列第5；小鹏汽车从第308位升至第141位，零跑汽车从第414位升至第187位。
insights.core: 全国工商联发布2026中国民营企业500强，营收总额44.93万亿元，同比增长4.35%；比亚迪、吉利跻身前十，小鹏、零跑排名大幅跃升。
insights.view: 头部与新势力车企规模快速扩张，意味着其在用户研究、产品体验与感官评测上的预算和能力将同步升级，行业人才与供应商竞争加剧；快消感官与CMI团队需警惕汽车等耐用消费品对消费者体验研究方法的跨界借鉴与争夺。
insights.action: 建议CMI团队梳理新能源车企的体验研究实践，评估其方法（如主观评测、场景化测试）对快消感官研究的可迁移性，并提前布局跨行业人才与合作资源。

insights.title: Omdia：2026年Q2全球TWS耳机出货量8210万台，同比下降0.7%
insights.summary: Omdia报告显示，2026年Q2全球TWS耳机出货量8210万台，同比下降0.7%，为三年多首次下滑。中国大陆市场出货同比降9.5%。开放式OWS耳机出货1110万台，同比涨12%，份额升至13.5%。苹果以20.5%份额居首，小米第二。
insights.core: Omdia数据显示2026年Q2全球TWS耳机出货8210万台，同比降0.7%，为三年多来首次下滑；中国大陆降9.5%；开放式OWS出货1110万台、同比增12%，份额升至13.5%；苹果以20.5%份额居首，小米第二。
insights.view: TWS进入存量博弈，增长动能向开放式OWS迁移，形态与佩戴体验正成为新的差异化抓手。对感官研究与CMI而言，需把评测框架从音质延展到佩戴舒适度、通透感与长时间佩戴的疲劳曲线，并关注中国需求疲软背后的换机周期与消费降级信号。
insights.action: 立即启动OWS专项感官与用户研究：建立佩戴舒适度与通透感的评价维度，追踪OWS与TWS用户的迁移路径与复购动因，为产品线布局与卖点沟通提供依据。

insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，能源巨头现金流是宏观成本与消费力的先行指标：现金流收缩往往预示物流与包材成本压力，进而影响产品定价与感官体验投入。
insights.action: 将此类宏观现金流数据纳入CMI监测看板，结合包材与物流成本，评估其对产品配方、包装质感及消费者价格敏感度的传导。

insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，后期融资收缩或扩张直接决定品牌方在消费者洞察、产品创新与感官测试上的预算弹性。资本趋紧时，企业更看重洞察投入的ROI与可落地性，CMI需从大样本研究转向敏捷、低成本、高预测力的方法。
insights.action: 建议追踪该数据季度变化，将其作为CMI预算规划的前瞻指标；若交易额持续走低，提前储备轻量化感官与消费者测试方案，并强化洞察对定价、口味与包装决策的直接支撑。

insights.action: 先补齐该预测的具体数据表与口径，再评估VR设备渗透率是否支撑虚拟货架、沉浸式感官测试试点；同步跟踪竞品在XR消费者研究上的应用案例，形成内部可行性判断。

insights.view: 对FMCG感官与CMI而言，移动游戏是注意力与碎片化场景的重要载体，其增长意味着品牌需关注游戏内广告、虚拟体验与感官联动的消费者触达机会，同时跨市场数据可辅助判断不同区域数字化消费节奏。
insights.action: 建议调取原数据表，重点拆解高增长区域与用户时长变化，评估游戏内植入、联名感官体验的可行性，并纳入下季度CMI场景化研究议程。

insights.title: 2021年12月-2025年12月中国互联网医疗用户使用率（附原数据表） ​​​
insights.summary: 2021年12月-2025年12月中国互联网医疗用户使用率（附原数据表） ​​​
insights.core: 该数据追踪2021年12月至2025年12月中国互联网医疗用户使用率变化，反映线上问诊、购药等数字健康服务的渗透趋势，是观察消费者健康行为线上化的重要指标。
insights.view: 对FMCG与雾化行业CMI而言，互联网医疗使用率上升意味着消费者健康信息获取与自我管理日益线上化，健康意识与合规诉求同步增强，将重塑尼古丁及功能性快消品的沟通语境与渠道逻辑。
insights.action: 建议将互联网医疗使用率纳入年度消费者健康趋势监测，交叉分析其与戒烟、减害类需求的关联，并据此调整数字渠道内容策略与合规沟通话术。

insights.action: 建议获取原数据表，按市场与人群拆分付费率，并与自身品类内容营销的转化数据交叉比对，评估微剧式短内容在品牌种草与感官叙事中的投放优先级。

insights.title: 第14届全国消费品行业CIO年会圆满闭幕！CIO组织2026年底、2027年活动计划重磅公布！
insights.summary: 2026年9月18日，第14届全国消费品行业CIO年会暨第6届中国企业数智化AI大会圆满成功闭幕!本次大会也是中国消费品行业CIO级别最高、影响力最大、规模最大的CIO大会，本次大会由数字精英俱乐部、全国消费品行业CIO组织、中国快消品人才网、AI人才网、中国企业数智化英才网、人工智能协会、企业家协会、全国各省市CIO
insights.core: 第14届全国消费品行业CIO年会暨第6届中国企业数智化AI大会于2026年9月18日闭幕，该会被定位为消费品行业CIO级别最高、规模最大的会议，并公布了CIO组织2026年底至2027年的活动计划。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，CIO年会规模升级说明数智化与AI正成为快消企业决策层核心议题。感官数据、消费者洞察的采集与分析将更依赖企业IT与数据中台能力，CMI需主动对接CIO体系以争取数据资源与工具支持。
insights.action: 建议CMI与感官研究负责人梳理内部数据链路痛点，主动联系企业CIO或数字化团队，争取将感官与消费者数据纳入数据中台规划，并关注CIO组织2026年底至2027年活动以获取跨界合作与标杆案例。

insights.title: 经合组织：2026年新西兰经济报告
insights.summary: 经合组织发布了“2026年新西兰经济报告”。新西兰经济正处于周期性复苏的早期阶段，受到强劲出口和货币宽松的推动。广泛的连贯性改革正开始解决新西兰长期生产率问题的根源。全球政策动荡、昂贵且不安全的电力、老龄化驱动的财政压力、投资缺口、资本市场深度不足以及有限的风险资本，都需要维持改革势头。
insights.core: 经合组织2026年新西兰经济报告指出，该国经济处于周期性复苏早期，出口强劲与货币宽松形成支撑，但电力成本高企、财政压力、投资缺口及资本市场深度不足等结构性问题仍需持续改革。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，新西兰消费市场短期回暖但结构性约束仍在。电力与资本成本压力可能传导至供应链与定价，消费者信心恢复缓慢，需警惕高端化与性价比需求并存的分化趋势，感官偏好或更偏向稳妥、熟悉的风味。
insights.action: 建议关注新西兰消费者信心与可支配收入变化，在感官测试中纳入价格敏感度与风险偏好维度，优先验证经典风味与高性价比产品概念，同时评估本地供应链成本波动对产品体验一致性的影响。

insights.title: 2026年4月南亚经济报告：与产业政策协同前行
insights.summary: 2025年的约7.0%回落至2026年的6.3%，印度仍是区域增长的核心引擎，其余经济体整体增速与其他新兴市场和发展中经济体基本持平。全球能源价格上涨、金融市场波动、人工智能冲击出口产业以及结构性改革推进缓慢，成为影响未来增长的重要变量。
insights.core: 南亚2026年增速由2025年的约7.0%回落至6.3%，印度仍是区域增长核心引擎，其余经济体增速与其他新兴市场大体持平；能源涨价、金融波动、AI冲击出口及结构性改革缓慢构成主要变量。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，南亚消费力扩张放缓但印度仍具结构性机会；能源与金融波动将放大价格敏感度，AI对出口产业的冲击或改变中产消费信心，感官偏好与性价比诉求需重新校准。
insights.action: 建议将印度与其余南亚市场分层研究，追踪能源价格与就业信心对购买频次的影响；在下轮感官测试中加入价格敏感与降级消费情境，验证风味与包装的价值感知韧性。

insights.title: Brand Finance：2026年泰国品牌50强
insights.summary: 2026年，泰国50大最具价值品牌的总品牌价值为450亿美元。 整体增长保持稳定，今年的排名突显了泰国领先品牌的韧性，尽管运营环境更具挑战性，仍有18个品牌实现了两位数的品牌价值增长。
insights.core: Brand Finance发布2026年泰国品牌50强，总品牌价值达450亿美元，整体增长稳定；在运营环境更具挑战的背景下，仍有18个品牌实现两位数品牌价值增长，凸显泰国领先品牌的韧性。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，泰国头部品牌在逆势中仍能实现两位数增值，说明其产品体验与消费者心智连接稳固。感官差异化和本土化风味偏好是品牌溢价的重要支撑，值得在东南亚市场研究中重点关注。
insights.action: 建议针对泰国市场开展感官偏好与品牌资产关联研究，识别高增长品牌的风味、口感及包装感官驱动因素，为区域产品创新与品牌定位提供依据。

insights.title: AI时代的科技高管重构：迈向持续增长
insights.summary: 79%的受访者将通过技术驱动可量化业务成果列为首要战略目标，高于数字监管合规与网络安全韧性（均为77%），人才建设占75%，数据能力和AI基础建设均达到74%。
insights.core: 该洞察显示，79%的科技高管将技术驱动可量化业务成果列为首要战略目标，超过数字监管合规、网络安全韧性、人才建设、数据能力与AI基础建设，表明企业正从技术投入转向以业务结果为导向的务实阶段。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，这意味着技术工具（如AI感官预测、消费者数据平台）的评估标准将更强调可量化的商业回报，而非单纯的技术先进性。CMI需主动证明自身洞察对销量、复购或新品成功率的直接贡献，否则在预算竞争中易被边缘化。
insights.action: 建议CMI团队立即梳理现有感官与消费者研究项目，建立与业务KPI（如转化率、市场份额）的量化关联，并优先试点AI辅助的快速感官筛选，用可验证的ROI案例争取技术预算与高层支持。

insights.title: CMR：2026年第一季度印度外置硬盘出货量同比增长42%
insights.summary: 印度的硬盘存储市场正迎来新的增长动力，这主要得益于消费者、中小型企业以及安防系统对大容量、高性价比存储设备需求的持续上升。2026年第一季度，外置硬盘出货量同比增长42%，而安防硬盘出货量则同比激增31%。
insights.core: 2026年第一季度印度外置硬盘出货量同比增长42%，安防硬盘增长31%，增长动力来自消费者、中小企业及安防系统对大容量、高性价比存储需求的持续上升。
insights.view: 对CMI而言，这一数据提示印度数字化基础设施与安防渗透正加速，消费者数据存储行为变化可能间接影响快消品线上触点与零售数字化节奏；但外置硬盘属科技硬件，与FMCG感官研究无直接关联，需警惕跨品类数据误用。
insights.action: 建议将印度存储需求增长作为宏观数字化信号纳入CMI监测，关注其是否带动电商、内容消费及智能家居场景，从而评估对快消品渠道与消费者触达的潜在影响。

insights.title: 杰兰路：2026年8月新能源二手车保值率特斯拉83.5%居首，环比上升
insights.summary: 杰兰路发布2026年8月新能源二手车价格与保值率月度报告，国内新能源品牌保值率分化明显。特斯拉以83.5%的保值率居首，理想以82.9%紧随其后，乐道与小米均为80.0%。方程豹、问界分别录得78.3%和77.3%。部分品牌下滑：智界保值率75.3%，环比下降0.3个百分点；阿维塔68.4%，环比回落0.8个百分点；一
insights.core: 杰兰路2026年8月报告显示，新能源二手车保值率分化加剧：特斯拉83.5%居首，理想82.9%紧随，乐道、小米均80.0%，而智界、阿维塔环比下滑。
insights.view: 保值率正成为消费者对品牌长期价值与产品体验的信任投票，与快消感官研究逻辑相通——用户体验一致性决定复购与残值。对CMI而言，需将保值率纳入品牌健康度追踪，作为产品力与用户口碑的滞后验证指标。
insights.action: 建议将保值率月度数据接入品牌资产看板，与用户满意度、NPS做相关性分析；针对下滑品牌，启动用户感知诊断，定位体验短板以支撑产品迭代。

insights.title: 国际机器人联合会：2025年全球工业及专业服务人形机器人销量约7000台
insights.summary: 国际机器人联合会数据显示，2025年全球工业及专业服务人形机器人销量约7000台。2024年常规工业机器人新装约54.2万台。部分人形机器人用于AI数据采集，汽车工厂仅小规模试点。美国银行预测2026年出货9万台，2030年达120万台。
insights.core: 国际机器人联合会数据显示，2025年全球工业及专业服务人形机器人销量约7000台，远低于2024年常规工业机器人54.2万台新装量；部分用于AI数据采集，汽车工厂仅小规模试点。美银预测2026年出货9万台、2030年达120万台。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官与CMI而言，人形机器人尚处早期数据采集与试点阶段，短期不构成消费者研究工具替代。但其数据采集定位值得关注：若未来用于标准化感官测试或消费场景观察，可能改变样本采集与行为数据获取方式。
insights.action: 建议CMI团队持续跟踪人形机器人在数据采集与零售场景的试点进展，评估其在消费者行为观察、货架互动测试中的可行性，暂不投入，先建立技术雷达与案例库。

insights.title: Omdia：2026年全球智能手机出货量预计10.97亿部，同比下降12%
insights.summary: Omdia预计，2026年全球智能手机出货量同比下降12%至10.97亿部，营收同比上涨12%至6516亿美元，平均售价同比上涨27%至594美元。低端机型占比将从40.6%降至25.6%，高端机型从21.1%升至28.4%，走向高端化。
insights.core: Omdia预计2026年全球智能手机出货量降至10.97亿部，同比降12%，但营收增12%至6516亿美元，均价涨27%至594美元；低端占比由40.6%降至25.6%，高端由21.1%升至28.4%，市场明显高端化。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官与CMI而言，这是消费分层加剧的明确信号：量减价增意味着用户更愿为可感知的品质与体验付费。感官研究应从成本项转为溢价引擎，聚焦高端人群的触感、风味、包装质感等差异化体验，并重新校准低端市场的取舍逻辑。
insights.action: 建议将CMI预算向高端细分与体验型指标倾斜，建立感官属性与支付意愿的关联模型；同步复盘低端产品线的感官投入回报，为高端化产品定义提供依据。

insights.title: Counterpoint：2026上半年全球四足机器人出货量近3.5万台，宇树科技以37%市占率居首
insights.summary: Counterpoint数据显示，2026上半年全球四足机器人出货量接近3.5万台，宇树科技以37%份额居首。在工业巡检领域智元以27.8%领先，宇树份额17.6%。上半年40%出货量流向行业场景，机构预测全年将首次突破9万台。
insights.core: Counterpoint数据显示，2026上半年全球四足机器人出货近3.5万台，宇树科技以37%份额居首；工业巡检领域智元以27.8%领先、宇树17.6%；上半年40%流向行业场景，全年预计首破9万台。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官与CMI而言，四足机器人正从演示走向行业落地，意味着线下零售巡检、货架监测、消费者行为追踪等场景将出现可规模化数据采集终端，感官测试的物理执行环节或被自动化重构，CMI数据源与样本获取方式面临升级。
insights.action: 建议CMI团队跟踪四足机器人在零售巡检与门店执行中的渗透节奏，评估其作为货架与陈列数据采集工具的可行性，并提前与相关厂商建立测试合作，验证数据质量与成本效益。

insights.title: 英伟达：2026财年员工均薪28.205万美元，黄仁勋总薪酬同比下降27%至3630万美元
insights.summary: 英伟达CEO黄仁勋近日表示，企业应尽可能多地支付员工薪酬。他亲自审查公司全部42000名员工的薪酬方案，并在100%的情况下增加薪酬支出。2026财年英伟达员工平均收入达28.205万美元，黄仁勋本人总薪酬3630万美元，同比下降约27%。
insights.core: 英伟达2026财年员工均薪28.205万美元，黄仁勋亲审全员薪酬并100%加薪，其个人总薪酬同比下降27%至3630万美元，体现高投入、重人才、创始人让利的组织信号。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官与CMI团队而言，这提示人才竞争已从快消延伸至科技巨头：高薪与强激励将推高研究、数据与AI人才成本。感官与消费者洞察属稀缺复合岗，若薪酬与成长空间不足，易被科技企业虹吸，影响团队稳定性与方法论迭代。
insights.action: 建议立即盘点感官/CMI关键岗位薪酬竞争力与职业路径，对标科技与快消头部；同时用AI工具提升研究效率，把预算从重复执行转向高价值洞察，以价值证明争取薪酬与编制。

insights.title: IDC：2026年Q2全球耳戴市场出货9613万台，同比增长5.4%
insights.summary: IDC发布2026年Q2全球可穿戴设备报告：全球耳戴市场出货9613万台，同比增长5.4%。开放式耳机出货1233万台，同比增长35.0%，耳夹式暴涨82.2%，在开放式耳机中占比超六成。传统耳挂式下滑5.1%，颈挂式仅增0.9%，市场加速转向耳夹式。
insights.core: IDC数据显示2026年Q2全球耳戴出货9613万台，同比增5.4%；开放式耳机增35%，其中耳夹式暴涨82.2%、占开放式超六成，传统耳挂式下滑5.1%，颈挂式仅增0.9%，市场加速向耳夹式迁移。
insights.view: 对感官与CMI而言，耳夹式爆发意味着佩戴形态变化正重塑触觉、夹持舒适度与长时间佩戴体验的评价体系；消费者从音质优先转向无感佩戴与场景兼容，传统耳挂品类需重新定义感官价值主张。
insights.action: 建议即刻补充耳夹式佩戴舒适度与夹持力感官测试模型，开展用户场景化佩戴时长与痛点CMI追踪，并将耳夹式纳入下一代产品感官基准与竞品对标库。

insights.title: 钟南山团队：2026年研究显示偶然检出肺结节人群中71.34%从不吸烟
insights.summary: 钟南山团队在《癌症科学进展》发表研究显示，基于16省23家医院10560名偶然检出肺结节受试者随访，71.34%从不吸烟，71.10%有二手烟暴露史，73.20%肺癌病例发生于传统非高危人群，67.28%无不适症状。研究提示二手烟、厨房油烟等为重要诱因。
insights.core: 钟南山团队基于16省23家医院10560名偶然检出肺结节受试者随访发现，71.34%从不吸烟，71.10%有二手烟暴露史，73.20%肺癌发生于传统非高危人群，67.28%无症状，提示二手烟、厨房油烟等为重要诱因。
insights.view: 该研究揭示传统'吸烟者'风险画像已不足以覆盖真实暴露人群，二手烟、厨房油烟等环境暴露成为关键变量。对FMCG感官与CMI而言，这意味着消费者健康风险认知正从'主动吸烟'转向'被动环境暴露'，电子烟及雾化品类需重新审视其减害叙事与场景化沟通策略。
insights.action: 建议将环境暴露（二手烟、厨房油烟）纳入消费者健康风险分层模型，在感官测试与CMI调研中增加暴露史与场景变量，为电子烟减害定位及差异化沟通提供数据支撑。

insights.title: 洛图科技：2026年8月中国电竞显示器线上市场均价1168元，同比上涨约7.0%
insights.summary: 洛图科技最新报告显示，2026年8月中国电竞显示器线上均价1168元，同比上涨约7.0%；销量58.8万台，同比下降4.7%；销额6.9亿元，同比增长2.0%。AI算力需求引发存储芯片涨价，带动显示器核心料件成本上行，预计后续售价维持高位。
insights.core: 洛图科技数据显示，2026年8月中国电竞显示器线上均价1168元、同比涨约7.0%，销量58.8万台降4.7%，销额6.9亿元增2.0%；AI算力推高存储芯片价格，成本上行致售价维持高位。
insights.view: 对CMI而言，这是典型成本驱动型涨价而非需求拉动，量跌额升意味着消费者对价格敏感度上升、购买决策更谨慎。感官与体验研究需关注涨价后用户对产品价值感知的变化，避免单纯参数竞争削弱溢价合理性。
insights.action: 建议立即启动价格敏感度与价值感知追踪，结合感官体验测试识别可支撑溢价的核心卖点；同步监测竞品定价与促销节奏，为后续产品组合与沟通策略提供依据。

insights.title: Omdia：预计2026年全球智能手机出货量10.97亿部，同比下降12%

insights.core: Omdia预测2026年全球智能手机出货量同比下降12%至10.97亿部，但营收上涨12%至6516亿美元，均价大涨27%至594美元；低端占比骤降、高端占比提升，换机周期拉长与二手分流推动结构性高端化。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官与CMI而言，量降价升意味着消费者更少但更挑剔，感官体验与品质信号成为高端溢价的关键证据。研究需从大众样本转向高价值人群，关注触感、材质、包装仪式感等可感知线索，并纳入二手与延保等替代行为对购买决策的干扰。
insights.action: 立即按价格带重构感官与CMI研究：高端线强化材质触感、开箱仪式与品质信号测试；低端线聚焦基础体验与成本感知。建立换机周期与二手分流的追踪指标，用高价值人群样本替代泛化调研。

insights.title: RD观测：2026年iPhone 18 Pro系列开售日销量32.28万台，同比增长约30%

insights.core: RD观测显示iPhone 18 Pro系列开售日销量32.28万台，达上代130%，同比增长约30%；Pro Max占55.5%，Pro占44.5%；新机搭载2nm A20 Pro芯片，持续性能提升40%。
insights.view: 高端机型首销强劲、Pro Max占比过半，印证消费者愿为可感知的性能与体验溢价买单。对FMCG感官与CMI而言，启示在于把抽象的'技术参数'转译为可感知的感官收益与场景价值，并关注高端化、大屏/强体验偏好的人群分层，用首销窗口验证概念与定价。
insights.action: 建议借新品首销窗口开展快速CMI追踪：拆解Pro与Pro Max人群画像与购买动因，测试'性能提升'对应的感官/体验语言，沉淀高端化沟通话术与定价敏感度基线，供后续品类概念与包装测试复用。

insights.core: 2026年8月中国智能门锁线上销量72.1万套，同比降3.2%、环比增19.3%；销额5.1亿元，同比降19.0%。小米销量份额居首，德施曼销额份额居首，头部品牌集中度下降。

insights.action: 建议立即建立量价与份额双维监测，对小米、德施曼及中腰部品牌做感官体验对标测试，识别价格敏感与体验敏感人群，指导产品定位与溢价策略。

insights.title: European retail in 2025 and 2026 What is the current state of the retail sector in Europe? The European retail landscape in 2025 and 2026 is shaped by a paradox: purchasing power continued to grow, inflation moved closer to the European Central Bank’s target, and labor markets remained resilient, yet consumer sentiment stayed cautious. Retail turnover increased, but continued to lag behind income growth as households adapted to years of economic uncertainty. The lasting effects of the pandemic, inflation, geopolitical tensions, and supply chain disruptions have fundamentally changed consumer behavior. Even as economic conditions improve, many Europeans remain price-conscious and increasingly focus on value, balancing affordability with quality, convenience, functionality, and trusted brands. This study examines the key trends shaping European retail in 2025 and 2026. It provides insights into purchasing power, retail turnover, retail share of private consumption, and inflation, helping to explain how changing spending priorities and renewed inflationary pressures are influencing consumer behavior across Europe. This study highlights how the retail sector in Europe has developed. In addition to well-founded brief analyses, the 20-page PDF also includes numerous maps and charts that present the content and data in a clear and comprehensible way. Download now Thank you for your interest! Download the complete study now as a PDF: European retail in 2025 and 2026 Some key results at a glance: Purchasing power In 2025, purchasing power across the EU continued to grow despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and elevated inflation in parts of Europe. Average per capita purchasing power reached 22,425 euros, representing a nominal increase of 3.3 percent compared to the revised 2024 figure. In total, residents of the 27 member states had approximately 10.1 trillion euros at their disposal for expenses such as food, retail purchases, housing, services, energy costs, private pensions, insurance, vacations, and mobility. The strongest increases were recorded in Poland (+8.8 percent), Lithuania (+8.3 percent), Romania (+7.7 percent), and Bulgaria (+7.3 percent), reflecting the continued economic convergence of Southern and Eastern European markets. Retail turnover After a robust 5.5 percent increase in 2023 and growth of 3.0 percent in 2024, the growth rate of retail turnover in the EU slowed further to 2.1 percent in 2025, reflecting the continued normalization of consumer spending patterns beyond the post-pandemic recovery. The strongest gains were recorded in Northern and Eastern Europe, led by Norway (+13.1 percent) and Lithuania (+10.5 percent), followed by Sweden (+8.9 percent), Bulgaria (+8.2 percent), and Slovakia (+8.0 percent). Rising wages and improving purchasing power supported retail spending across these markets. By contrast, large Western European markets remain weak and continue to hold back overall growth, with the United Kingdom even recording a decline of -0.6 percent. “The key finding is not that Europeans are spending less, but that they are spending differently. Retail turnover continues to grow, yet an increasing share of consumer budgets is flowing into services and experiences. This points to a structural shift in spending priorities across Europe. Rising purchasing power no longer translates automatically into higher retail spending.” — Philipp Willroth, Study Lead, NIQ Geomarketing Retail share of private consumption Retail’s share of total private consumption in the EU declined for the fourth consecutive year in 2025, falling to 31.9 percent. While purchasing power and retail turnover increased, consumers continued to allocate a larger share of their budgets to services, travel, leisure, and hospitality. Significant regional differences persist across the EU. Croatia recorded the highest retail share at 48.3 percent, followed by Lithuania (45.7 percent), Bulgaria (44.0 percent), and Hungary (43.2 percent). Germany ranked last with just 22.2 percent of total consumer spending directed toward retail purchases. Inflation After the sharp price increases seen in the years following the 2022 energy crisis, inflation across the EU stabilized further in 2025, averaging 2.5 percent and coming close to the European Central Bank's target. The highest rates were recorded in Romania (6.8 percent), followed by Estonia (4.8 percent), Hungary (4.4 percent), Croatia (4.4 percent), and Slovakia (4.2 percent), reflecting continued wage growth and labor market pressures in parts of Eastern Europe. By contrast, France reported one of the lowest inflation rates in Europe, at just 0.9 percent, supported by weaker domestic demand and a favorable energy mix. In 2026, inflation in the EU-27 is expected to rise again to 3.1 percent, driven primarily by renewed pressure on energy markets. Download the complete study now for free! insights.title: The Return of Consumer Choice in Eastern Europe Smart Beauty Starts Here What It Means for FMCG Growth Eastern Europe's FMCG market is entering a new phase. After a prolonged period in which inflation shaped both consumer behavior and market performance, growth is increasingly being driven by a different force: consumer choice. As pricing pressures begin to ease across much of the region, consumers are regaining flexibility in how they spend. But rather than returning to pre-inflation habits, they are becoming more deliberate about what deserves a place in their baskets and what doesn't. Yet the return of consumer demand does not mean a return to old habits. If anything, the past few years have created a more thoughtful, deliberate shopper. Consumers have become accustomed to evaluating purchases more carefully, comparing alternatives, seeking value, and questioning whether products genuinely deserve a place in their baskets. As economic conditions gradually improve, many are spending more freely than before, but they are not spending blindly. The result is a new consumer reality where selectivity is becoming one of the most important drivers of FMCG growth. Consumers Are Returning, But Differently Across Eastern Europe, signs of a healthier growth environment are beginning to emerge. In several markets, growth is increasingly supported by underlying consumption rather than price increases alone. Markets such as Greece and Lithuania are demonstrating stronger demand fundamentals, with consumers buying more rather than simply paying more. This matters because it signals more than an economic recovery. It suggests consumers are regaining confidence and returning to categories and occasions that may have been deprioritized during periods of heightened inflation. However, this recovery remains uneven. While some households are benefiting from improving economic conditions, others continue to navigate affordability challenges. Across the region, manufacturers and retailers are operating in markets moving at very different speeds. The implication is clear: relying on regional averages is becoming increasingly risky. Understanding local market dynamics has never been more important. Value Has Become a Habit  One of the most significant legacies of the inflation era is that consumers have learned new shopping behaviors, and many of them appear to be sticking. Value-oriented retail formats continue to perform strongly in several markets. In Poland, discounters account for more than 45% of FMCG value sales, highlighting the continued importance of affordability and value-driven shopping habits. Private label is also maintaining momentum across parts of the region. In Bulgaria, private label continues to significantly outperform the broader market, while in Slovakia, consumers remain focused on affordability and value-led purchasing decisions. Importantly, these trends should not be interpreted as consumers simply trading down. Rather, they reflect shoppers who have become more confident about evaluating alternatives. During years of inflation, many consumers experimented with different brands, retailers, and price tiers. In doing so, they discovered that value doesn't always mean compromise. As a result, competition has intensified, and consumers are increasingly willing to switch when they do not perceive sufficient added value. For brands, that creates both risk and opportunity. Loyalty is no longer guaranteed. Every product must continue earning its position. The New Battleground Is Perceived Value Perhaps the most important shift taking place across Eastern Europe is that consumers are becoming more selective in how they spend. The question is no longer whether shoppers are willing to pay more. They often are. The real question is whether they believe a product deserves it. Consumers continue to invest in products that offer meaningful benefits, whether those benefits are linked to quality, convenience, performance, trust, health, or personal relevance. At the same time, they are increasingly willing to seek alternatives in categories where differentiation is less obvious. This selectivity can be seen across multiple markets. It is visible in the continued success of private label, the growing importance of promotions, and the increasing willingness of consumers to reassess long-standing purchasing habits. It also reflects a broader global trend identified in A Tale of Two Consumers: consumers are becoming less predictable and more context-driven in their decision-making. The same shopper may actively seek savings in one category while happily paying more in another. This makes understanding category dynamics, shopping missions, and consumer motivations increasingly important for growth. Why Digital Commerce Is Amplifying the Shift Digital commerce is adding another dimension to these changing behaviors. While e-commerce penetration in Eastern Europe still trails some more developed digital markets, online channels continue to expand across the region and remain an important growth engine. Regional e-commerce value growth reached 4.4%, while individual markets such as Czechia, Romania, and Greece continue to post strong online momentum. What matters most is not simply the growth of the channel itself, but the behavior it encourages. Online environments give consumers greater visibility into pricing, broader access to assortment, easier comparison between brands, and more opportunities to discover alternatives. In many ways, digital commerce reinforces the behaviors consumers developed during recent years of economic uncertainty: comparison, evaluation, and thoughtful decision-making. As e-commerce continues to expand, products will increasingly compete on clearly communicated value rather than familiarity alone. For manufacturers and retailers, that raises the importance of product content, positioning, promotions, pricing strategies, and digital shelf execution. Looking Ahead: A Signal From Global Markets Although Eastern Europe is not yet displaying the same level of consumer polarization seen in some mature markets, early signals are beginning to emerge. Globally, NIQ research shows consumers increasingly moving between premium and value mindsets depending on category, occasion, and perceived benefit. Rather than behaving as consistently "premium" or consistently "budget-conscious" shoppers, consumers are fluidly switching between both approaches. Eastern Europe has not reached that point to the same extent. But many of the ingredients are already visible: stronger private label acceptance, continued value-seeking, growing digital transparency, and increasingly selective spending behaviors. For manufacturers and retailers planning, this is an important trend to watch. The next chapter of FMCG growth in Eastern Europe is unlikely to be defined by inflation. It will be defined by consumer choice. And growth will increasingly belong to the brands that understand not simply what consumers are buying, but why they believe certain products are worth paying for. insights.title: From Deep Cleaning to Autonomous Cleaning For decades, the vacuum cleaner category was largely defined by a single consumer need: cleaning the home. Today, that definition is no longer sufficient. New insights from NIQ suggest Australia's vacuum market is evolving into a more complex ecosystem of distinct consumer missions, where shoppers are not simply choosing a vacuum cleaner, but choosing a cleaning philosophy. The category is fragmenting into three clear strategic spaces:  Convenience-led cleaning represented by stick vacuums.  Automation-led cleaning represented by robot vacuums.  Performance-led cleaning represented by upright and canister vacuums.   For manufacturers and retailers, understanding these missions may be more important than understanding the category itself.  The Category Is Growing Through Upgrades, Not Adoption The first strategic observation is that vacuum cleaners have become a mature replacement market. Approximately 65% of purchases are replacement driven, while 28% are motivated by consumers upgrading their current solution. Only 4% are first-time purchases. This means most shoppers already understand the category and enter the market with experience. They know what annoys them about their current product. They know what they want improved. The opportunity is therefore not to convince consumers to buy a vacuum cleaner. It is to convince them to buy a better solution to an existing problem. The upgrade mentality creates fertile ground for innovation and premiumisation, particularly when brands can clearly articulate how their products make cleaning easier, faster or more effective. Mission One: Convenience Is Driving the Rise of Stick Vacuums Stick vacuums have emerged as the dominant sub-category in the study, representing more than half of surveyed purchasers. What makes these buyers distinctive is not necessarily a demand for premium technology, but a desire for frictionless cleaning. Compared with other segments, stick vacuum shoppers place strong emphasis on: Price transparency  Promotional offers  Comparing models and features  Trust in established brands  Everyday convenience benefits  This consumer is looking for balance. They want a vacuum that performs well enough while fitting seamlessly into daily life. The goal is not necessarily achieving the deepest clean. It is making cleaning less of a chore. For marketers, this means leading with use cases rather than specifications. Messaging around quick clean-ups, lightweight design, cordless freedom and ease of storage is likely to resonate more strongly than purely technical performance claims. The winning brands in this segment are simplifying household routines. Mission Two: Robot Vacuums Are Creating an Automation Economy The most strategically interesting segment may be robot vacuums. While smaller than the stick segment, robot vacuum buyers display a fundamentally different mindset. They over-index on product quality and feature-led decision-making compared with the total category. Unlike traditional vacuum shoppers, these consumers are not merely purchasing a cleaning product. They are purchasing an outcome which is cleaning without participation. This represents a shift from product utility to lifestyle automation. The study shows robot vacuum shoppers are more heavily influenced by: Product functionality  Feature comparisons  Reviews and recommendations  Smart capabilities and innovation cues  Interestingly, they are less reliant on traditional brand image cues than the wider category. Instead, performance and technology become the primary trust signals. This creates a strategic lesson that extends far beyond vacuum cleaners. Across many consumer technology categories, the premium is increasingly attached to time savings rather than product ownership itself. Consumers are not paying for a robot vacuum. They are paying for one less task on their weekly to-do list. Brands that position robot vacuums as part of the connected home ecosystem rather than as cleaning appliances may be better positioned for future growth. Mission Three: Performance Still Matters Despite excitement around cordless and autonomous solutions, traditional cleaning performance remains highly relevant. The report shows upright vacuum purchasers stand out for one critical reason that they are the most need-driven buyers in the category. Nearly three-quarters say their chosen product simply "meets my needs," significantly above the category average. They also over-index on quality, trust and reliability. These consumers are not chasing innovation for innovation's sake. They are focused on outcomes. For larger homes, pet owners and consumers with demanding cleaning requirements, cleaning performance remains the most important metric. This segment reminds us that disruption rarely eliminates consumer needs. Instead, it creates multiple pathways to satisfy them. The enduring relevance of upright and canister products suggests there will continue to be substantial demand for solutions built around cleaning power, durability and household-specific requirements. Research Has Become the New Battleground Regardless of segment, one behaviour unites vacuum shoppers. They research extensively. The report finds 84% of consumers conduct pre-purchase research before buying, with most actively seeking information on pricing, functionality, reviews, promotions and product comparisons. This finding has important implications. The vacuum purchase journey increasingly resembles a consumer electronics purchase journey rather than a traditional appliance purchase. Consumers want:  Proof  Validation  Expert guidance  User reviews  Side-by-side comparisons  In this environment, winning the search journey may be just as important as winning the shelf. Brands that invest in educational content, comparison tools and retailer content partnerships are likely to gain an advantage before shoppers even enter a store. The Store Is Still Where Decisions Are Finalised One of the most surprising findings is that despite the growth of digital research, physical retail remains dominant. Nearly 70% of vacuum purchases still happen in-store. This highlights a critical reality for manufacturers. The journey is digital-first but not digital-only. Consumers may begin with Google or AI searches, retailer websites and reviews, but many still want a physical validation step before committing. Touching the product. Assessing the weight. Comparing the build quality. Seeking reassurance from staff. The brands that create seamless connections between online discovery and in-store conversion will be best positioned to capture demand. The Future of the Category Is About Missions, Not Products The traditional way of viewing the category divides the market by product type. A more useful approach may be to divide it by consumer mission. The Australian vacuum market is increasingly composed of: Consumers seeking convenience.  Consumers seeking automation.  Consumers seeking performance.   Each group researches differently. Each group responds to different value propositions. Each group defines premium in a different way. The brands that continue marketing all vacuums the same way risk missing the deeper shifts occurring beneath the category. The future winners will be those that stop asking, "What type of vacuum are we selling?" And start asking, "What cleaning mission are we helping consumers achieve?" Source: NIQ Purchase Insights+ vacuum cleaner Study 2025, Australia (n=304 recent purchasers).  Purchase Insights+ Get inside the mind of your consumers. insights.title: The retailer brand is now just a brand – and it innovates like one Across Western Europe, nearly one in two new products now carries a retailer's name and the ambition behind them has changed. For years, the private label (retail brand) story was a price story. Trade down, trade back, repeat. The 2026 data tells a different one. Across France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK, innovation value sales were essentially flat over the latest 52 weeks — down 0.2%. But underneath that stillness, the market moved. Branded innovation grew 1.8% while private label innovation fell 2.1%. Read quickly, that looks like brands winning back the ground. Read properly, it's the first real test of whether retailer brands can behave like brands, because they're now operating at brand scale. The scale is the point. Private label accounted for 42% of innovation launches a year ago compared to 46% today. More than 83,000 new private label products reached the shelf this year, and retailers expanded their own assortments faster than the total FMCG shelf: +2.5% versus +1.6%, rising to +3.3% in Spain and +3.2% in Germany. Shelf space is being reallocated, not just contested. The advantage is real and narrowing Innovation contributes 11.7% of private label value versus 8.1% for branded products. That's a meaningful gap, and it holds almost everywhere: Germany is the extreme at 16.9% versus 9.6%, with Spain at 11.0% versus 5.5%. Italy is the one market where the advantage has gone and where branded and private label sit at parity. A year ago, though, the private label figure was 12.2%, while branded held flat at 8.1%. The lead is still substantial. It just isn't growing anymore, and the reason sits in velocity, where private label innovation fell 6.9% against a market decline of 1.6%. More launches, less traction from each one. Scale has been achieved; productivity is the open question. Which raises a more uncomfortable one for both sides of the shelf: if a retailer can now match a brand on volume of innovation but not yet on the return from it, is the constraint the pipeline itself, or the decision about what deserves to be in it? Premiumization is already happening, just not where you'd expect The most interesting signal is in pricing. On average, a new private label product is priced 9% above the typical private label item on shelf. Retailers are no longer launching only to defend the entry tier, they are using new products to reach up. Home Care is the clearest example, and the most nuanced. New private label products in the category still sell at a 21% premium to the average private label item. A year ago that premium was 38%. The premium hasn't disappeared, it has come down, as private label innovation prices in Home Care fell 12.3% year on year. In other words: retailers built a genuine premium tier here, and are now making it more accessible. The opposite is happening elsewhere. Private label innovation prices rose 5.7% in Personal Care and 5.1% in Confectionery & Snacks — the two categories where private label innovation is growing fastest, up 11.5% and 23.9% in value. Higher prices and faster growth in the same place is not a discount strategy. Meanwhile Food, that represent 72% of the private label pipeline, declined 4.4%, and its innovation intensity slipped from 23% to 20% of items. The volume is in one place; the growth is in another. Who are you competing with in 2027? If you are a manufacturer, the competitive question goes from "how do we defend against a cheaper copy?" to "what happens when the retailer brand innovates faster, prices higher and takes more of its growth from new products than we do?" That changes what a 2027 plan needs to answer. Is the portfolio built for a competitor that now occupies the middle and the premium tier, not just the entry one? Where are you defending share with a product that hasn't genuinely changed in years and would renovating it do more than another line extension? If innovation is carrying 11.7% of our competitor's growth and 8.1% of ours, is the gap in our pipeline, or in what we choose to launch? If you are a retailer, the question is harder: you are launching more and getting less from each launch. Which half of that pipeline is earning its space, and what would you stop doing to fund the half that works? Both answers depend on the same thing: knowing which innovations work before they hit the shelf. Want to see the full report? Get in touch September 21 2026
