你有没有经历过自己的辛勤付出——包括那些成功——却被上司忽视？TED的新播客《可修复的》正是为此而生——来解决那些打电话倾诉工作烦恼的普通人的问题。
在第四集中，联合主持人、顶尖领导力教练弗朗西斯·弗雷和安妮·莫里斯认识了奈娅，这位来电者在一次重大重组后与新上任且心不在焉的老板搭档，难以获得认可。奈娅拼尽全力把工作做好，但缺乏认可和鼓励——甚至老板根本不知道她在做什么——让她逐渐失去了动力。
弗朗西斯和安妮给奈娅的第一条建议很简单：看到事情中的人性——也看到你老板的人性。
“有时候，阻碍你成为老板的好搭档的原因，可能是你对现状还残留着一些不满，”安妮解释道。“但这种情绪对你没有帮助。”
相反，她们鼓励奈娅认识到老板也是普通人，并原谅他们犯的错误。
弗朗西斯和安妮还分享了这个策略让她练习：选择好奇而非评判。
弗朗西斯是这样说的：“你可以在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者不可能同时存在。所以如果你对老板抱有评判，你就无法真正对他的处境感到好奇。当你把老板看作一个身兼多职的人时，我们怎么帮他创造条件走向成功？”
“好奇最简单的表达方式——这在工作场所中真是一剂神奇的灵药——就是以提问的形式呈现，”安妮说。比如，你可以先问老板，什么方式最方便他了解你的成果和贡献。或者，你可以聚焦于如何让你们之间的会议更高效，问他：“我们的一对一时间怎样才能服务于我们共同想达成的目标？”
另一个选择：坦诚说出你的担忧，问老板他眼中你的成功是什么样的。你可以这样说：“我的担忧是：我工作非常努力，但在这种变动时期，我怕六个月过去了，大家会怀疑我到底有没有做好。所以对我来说，明确一点会很有帮助——什么是做好，我怎样才能帮你获取这些信息？”
在各个行业、世界各地，许多人都正在经历职场重组和其他大规模变革。和奈娅一样，对正在发生的事情感到焦虑和压力、需要一段调整期，都是正常的。

##带着问题去沟通——把老板视为与你协作的另一个人——能帮你找回一些主动权和自主性。

弗朗西斯说：“试着做你能做的事，然后惊叹于对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一份你希望对方如何改变的清单。我觉得你会惊喜地发现——这正是这件事最美妙的部分。”

无论你从事什么工作或行业，你都能在《Fixable》中找到可操作的实用建议，改善你的工作日。在其他期节目中，你还能学到如何克服沟通障碍、扩展副业规模，以及主持更高效的会议。另外：点击这里，有机会在节目中获得你自己工作问题的解答！现在就在你常用的播客平台收听《Fixable》。

readings.title: Why are more Americans moving to Ireland?
body: 15 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Anne Cassidy In a historic reversal, the number of Americans moving to Ireland last year was higher than the number of Irish people migrating to the US. Was this just a blip or the start of a more profound trend? Michael Sable is an American stand-up comedian and communications manager who moved from Washington DC to Dublin in 2016.  Sable, who draws on his experience of being an American living in the Republic of Ireland in his stand-up routine, says that, when he first arrived, many Irish people he met were surprised he'd made the move, but now they don't question it.  "I've noticed that, as the years go on, people have been less and less incredulous when hearing that an American moved to Ireland," he says.  Sable is one of a rising number of people who have moved to Ireland from the US, with the latest data showing the figure nearly doubling from  4,900 to 9,600 between 2024 and 2025 ,  exceeding the number of Irish people headed in the opposite direction.   It comes as the US saw more people leave than arrive last year, according to a report from US think tank the  Brookings Institution . It said this was the first time that this had been the case "in at least half a century".  The think tank highlighted "dramatic changes in immigration policy" under the second administration of President Trump, including more removals of undocumented foreign workers, and the White House "all but suspend[ing]" the US programme for accepting refugees.    Separately, more American citizens are choosing to move abroad than ever before, says the  Wall Street Journal.  It calculated that "at least 180,000 Americans" voluntarily left the US in 2025, which it said was a record high.   The reversal in the flow of migration between Ireland and the US marks a historic turning point in the shared history of the two countries, which have deep-rooted ties.  For centuries, millions of Irish people emigrated to the US in search of work or a better life, making Irish Americans one of the country's largest ethnic groups. There have been several US presidents with Irish ancestry, including John F Kennedy and Joe Biden, whose visits to Ireland were  celebrated more like homecomings  than diplomatic missions.   Irish writer Colm Tóibín has frequently explored the relationship between Ireland and the US in his work, particularly in his novels, Brooklyn and Long Island, which follow the story of an Irish girl who emigrates to America in the 1950s.  Tóibín, who lives in the US, says the relationship between the US and Ireland has changed. "A myth was created that America was a great place of opportunity and wealth," he says. "It was built into the [Irish] culture that if there's any trouble, you go to England, if there's any ambition or spark you go to America." "The flow of young people [from Ireland to the US] looking for work just hasn't continued. So, that is going to be a big change in the future, because you're not going to get the same easy connection between Ireland and America," he adds.  The trend partly reflects political shifts in both countries. As well as developing into a high-tech, export-driven knowledge economy, Ireland has undergone a social transformation in recent decades, moving from a deeply conservative society to a liberal, progressive nation, following referendums on divorce, abortion and gay marriage.    Tóibín, who was a prominent campaigner for the "yes" vote in Ireland’s same-sex marriage referendum, says: "Everyone became more aware that Ireland was a more liberal, cosmopolitan, open society, and that it would be a good place to live." By contrast, the US has moved to the political right under President Trump, who, since returning to office, has launched a major crackdown on illegal immigration.   Tóibín revisits the Irish-American immigrant experience in his latest short story collection, The News from Dublin. In one story in the collection, Five Bridges, the protagonist is an undocumented Irish immigrant preparing to leave America before US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as Ice, come looking for him. The number of Irish citizens deported from the US  rose by more than 50%  in 2025.  "There are large numbers of Irish people in America who are official in every way – they pay taxes, own their own house, have kids in school, but they came in on a tourist visa," says Tóibín. "If Ice found them, Ice would detain them. That's really frightening." Expatsi, a firm that helps US citizens to move abroad,  reported it experienced a month's worth of traffic  in the hours after President Trump's election in 2024. Expatsi co-founder Jen Barnett says the reasons Americans cite for leaving are wide-ranging. "[Factors include] what's going on politically in the US, and has been for 10 years, the cost of living, and then safety. Gun violence is so prevalent," she says.  Politics was also a driving factor for Kevin Wozniak, an American lecturer living in Ireland. He and his husband left Boston in 2023 after he got a post at Maynooth University, 23km (14 miles) west of Dublin.  "My motivation to look at opportunities abroad was deep fears about the trajectory of the country in the era of Donald Trump," Wozniak says. "Ireland has liberalised very significantly and has moved in exactly the opposite direction that the US is moving." Natalia Lange, a migrant support worker based in Crosshaven, county Cork, moved there from Michigan with her husband after the 2024 US election. Lange, who is half-Hungarian and has an EU passport, dreamed of living in Ireland since visiting on a school trip. "Politically, Ireland aligns much more with how we think," she says. "The US has the infrastructure to take in a lot more people, but it's a lot less inviting." Lauren Udoh, from Houston, Texas, moved to Claregalway, in county Galway, in 2021 after marrying her Irish husband. Udoh, who has two young children, works as an executive assistant and documents expat life on social media under the moniker TheGalwayGal.  "One of the biggest benefits is safety. I feel a lot safer here," she says. "With kids going to school, you don’t have to worry about school shootings." Emigration from Ireland has fallen, with 65,600 people leaving in the year to April 2025, a  6% decrease on 2024 , according to the Irish Central Statistics Office (CSO). For those wanting to live abroad, Australia is the most popular destination.  The CSO said 13,500 people left Ireland for Australia in the year to April 2025, the highest level since 2013. This is more than double the estimated 6,100 people who left Ireland for the US, which was, however, still up 22% on the previous year.   Restrictions around J1 visas, which allow Irish university students to work and travel in the US, has caused many  Irish students to rethink studying in the US.    Karen McHugh, CEO at Safe Home Ireland, an organisation supporting Irish-born emigrants wishing to return to Ireland, says: "We've certainly noticed an increase in queries about returning [from the US to Ireland]," she says. "Australia and Canada are two major countries where people are now going to from Ireland, and that's ease of getting a visa." Irish student Jamie McElhinney is currently on a work placement in Portugal as part of his hospitality management course. McElhinney, who studies at Dundalk Institute of Technology, says current immigration controls put him off seeking a work placement in the US. "I was going to go to Boston, and then all of the news about Ice started coming out. It’s a deterrent from going over there," he says.  While there are opportunities in Ireland, with  employment at 74.4%,  there is also a growing housing crisis, with recent  protests  over the shortage of affordable housing.  Barnett says the housing shortage is something the Americans her company helps to relocate are mindful of, adding: "They don't want to add to [the housing crisis], so one of the things we talk to them about is staying out of city centres." Sable, whose Irish grandparents emigrated to the US in 1939, is one of many Americans whose ancestry enabled them to get an Irish passport. Applications for Irish passports in the US rose by 10% in 2024 , the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs reported.  Sable now thinks of Ireland as home. "Culturally, I identify a lot more with Irish people," he says. "It's a very collective society, not huge on individualism like in the US." More like this:  •  Why Ireland's film industry is booming    •  Is New York's cannabis business flying high?   •  The 'brutal' toll of war on Dubai’s tourist trade Bill Hillyard, another American with Irish roots, relocated to Ireland for the cooler climate. He and his wife Anne left California following wildfires in 2019. "My wife said we need to move somewhere where it rains." They now run a pub called The Algiers in Baltimore, Co Cork.  Hillyard says he now tries to avoid turbulent events in the US. "I tried not to follow the news because I'm here now," he says. "But I'm reminded every day, because everyone asks me about Trump and what's going on there… I'm West Cork's ambassador to the US at this point." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. ##段落
去年，移居爱尔兰的美国人数量超过了移居美国的爱尔兰人，这是一次历史性的逆转。这只是一时的反常现象，还是一个更深刻趋势的开端？

##段落
迈克尔·塞布尔是一位美国单口喜剧演员兼传播经理，2016年从华盛顿特区搬到了都柏林。塞布尔将自己在爱尔兰共和国生活的美国人经历融入脱口秀表演中。他说，初到爱尔兰时，许多他遇到的爱尔兰人都对他做出这一决定感到惊讶，但如今人们已经不再质疑了。

##段落
“我注意到，随着时间推移，人们听到美国人移居爱尔兰时，越来越不那么难以置信了，”他说。

##段落
塞布尔是从美国移居爱尔兰的人数不断增长的一个缩影。最新数据显示，这一数字在2024年至2025年间几乎翻了一番，从4900人增至9600人，超过了反向移居美国的爱尔兰人数量。

##段落
与此同时，根据美国智库布鲁金斯学会的一份报告，去年离开美国的人数超过了进入美国的人数。报告称，这是“至少半个世纪以来”首次出现这种情况。

##段落
该智库重点指出了特朗普总统第二任期内“移民政策的剧烈变化”，包括加大了对无证外籍工人的遣返力度，以及白宫“几乎暂停了”美国接收难民的计划。

##段落
另外，《华尔街日报》称，越来越多的美国公民选择移居海外。该报估算，“至少18万美国人”在2025年自愿离开了美国，称这是历史最高纪录。

##段落
爱尔兰与美国之间移民流向的逆转，标志着两国共同历史中的一个历史性转折点。两国有着根深蒂固的纽带。

##段落
几个世纪以来，数百万爱尔兰人移民到美国寻求工作或更好的生活，使爱尔兰裔美国人成为美国最大的族裔群体之一。美国有多位总统拥有爱尔兰血统，包括约翰·F·肯尼迪和乔·拜登，他们对爱尔兰的访问更像是回乡探亲，而非外交使命。

##段落
爱尔兰作家科尔姆·托宾在其作品中频繁探讨爱尔兰与美国的关系，尤其是在他的小说《布鲁克林》和《长岛》中，讲述了一位1950年代移民美国的爱尔兰女孩的故事。

##段落
现居美国的托宾表示，美国与爱尔兰之间的关系已经发生了变化。“人们创造了一个神话，认为美国是一个充满机遇和财富的好地方，”他说。“这已经融入了（爱尔兰）文化——如果遇到麻烦，你去英国；如果有任何抱负

##“或者‘火花’（spark），你就去美国。”“年轻人（从爱尔兰到美国）找工作的潮流并没有延续下去。所以，未来这将是一个巨大的变化，因为你不会再看到爱尔兰和美国之间那种轻而易举的联系了，”他补充道。这一趋势部分反映了两国的政治变迁。爱尔兰不仅发展成了高科技、出口驱动的知识经济体，近几十年来还经历了一场社会变革——在离婚、堕胎和同性婚姻公投之后，从一个极度保守的社会转变为一个自由、进步的国家。托宾曾是爱尔兰同性婚姻公投中“赞成”阵营的知名活动人士，他说：“每个人都越来越意识到，爱尔兰是一个更自由、更国际化、更开放的社会，会是一个宜居的好地方。”相比之下，美国在特朗普总统治下转向了政治右翼。特朗普重返白宫后，发起了对非法移民的大规模打击。托宾在最新短篇小说集《来自都柏林的消息》中重新审视了爱尔兰裔美国移民的经历。其中一篇《五座桥》的主人公是一名无证爱尔兰移民，正准备在美国移民和海关执法局（ICE）找上门之前离开美国。2025年，被美国驱逐出境的爱尔兰公民人数上升了超过50%。“在美国有大量爱尔兰人在各方面都是合法的——他们纳税、拥有自己的房子、孩子在上学，但他们是持旅游签证入境的，”托宾说。“如果ICE找到他们，ICE就会拘留他们。那真的很可怕。”帮助美国公民移居海外的公司Expatsi报告称，2024年特朗普当选后的数小时内，其网站流量相当于平时一个月的量。Expatsi联合创始人珍·巴内特表示，美国人给出的离开理由五花八门。“（因素包括）美国政治上正在发生的事，而且已经持续了10年，还有生活成本，然后是安全。枪支暴力太普遍了，”她说。政治也是居住在爱尔兰的美国讲师凯文·沃兹尼亚克离开的驱动因素。2023年，他和丈夫在获得都柏林以西23公里（14英里）处梅努斯大学的职位后离开了波士顿。“我寻求海外机会的动机，是对唐纳德·特朗普时代这个国家发展轨迹的深切恐惧，”沃兹尼亚克说。“爱尔兰已经非常显著地自由化了，正朝着与美国完全相反的方向前进。”娜塔莉亚·兰格是科克郡克罗斯黑文的一名移民支持工作者，2024年美国大选后与丈夫从密歇根搬到了那里。兰格有一半匈牙利血统，持有欧盟护照，梦想在爱尔兰生活。

## 她是在一次学校旅行中访问这里后决定留下的。“在政治上，爱尔兰与我们的理念契合得多，”她说，“美国有接纳更多人的基础设施，但远没有那么友好。”来自得克萨斯州休斯顿的劳伦·乌多，在嫁给她的爱尔兰丈夫后，于2021年搬到了戈尔韦郡的克莱尔戈尔韦。乌多有两个年幼的孩子，担任行政助理，并以“TheGalwayGal”的网名在社交媒体上记录外籍生活。“最大的好处之一是安全。我在这里感觉安全多了，”她说，“孩子上学，你不用担心中学枪击事件。”根据爱尔兰中央统计局（CSO）的数据，爱尔兰的移出人数有所下降，截至2025年4月的一年中有65,600人离开，比2024年减少了6%。对于想移居国外的人来说，澳大利亚是最受欢迎的目的地。CSO表示，截至2025年4月的一年中，有13,500人离开爱尔兰前往澳大利亚，为2013年以来的最高水平。这一数字是估计约6,100名前往美国的爱尔兰人的两倍多，不过后者仍比上年增长了22%。J1签证（允许爱尔兰大学生在美国工作和旅行）的相关限制，已导致许多爱尔兰学生重新考虑赴美学习。Safe Home Ireland是一家为希望返回爱尔兰的爱尔兰裔移民提供支持的组织，其首席执行官凯伦·麦休说：“我们确实注意到有关（从美国返回爱尔兰）的咨询有所增加。”她说：“澳大利亚和加拿大是人们现在从爱尔兰前往的两个主要国家，因为签证容易获得。”爱尔兰学生杰米·麦克尔希尼目前正在葡萄牙进行工作实习，这是他酒店管理课程的一部分。就读于邓多克理工学院的麦克尔希尼说，当前的移民管控让他不愿去美国寻求工作实习。“我本来要去波士顿，后来所有关于Ice的新闻开始出来。这让人不敢去那里，”他说。虽然爱尔兰存在机会，就业率达到74.4%，但也存在日益严重的住房危机，近期还因经济适用房短缺而爆发抗议。巴尼特说，住房短缺是她公司帮助搬迁的美国人会留意的问题，并补充道：“他们不想加剧（住房危机），所以我们与他们谈论的一件事就是不要住在市中心。”萨布尔的爱尔兰祖父母于1939年移居美国，他是许多因血统而获得爱尔兰护照的美国人之一。爱尔兰外交部报告称，2024年在美国的爱尔兰护照申请量上升了10%。萨布尔现在把爱尔兰视为家。“在文化上，我更认同爱尔兰人，”他说，“这是一个非常……

## 集体社会，不像美国那样崇尚个人主义。”更多类似内容： • 为什么爱尔兰电影产业正在蓬勃发展 • 纽约的大麻生意是否蒸蒸日上？ • 战争对迪拜旅游业的“残酷”冲击 另一位有爱尔兰血统的美国人比尔·希利亚德为了更凉爽的气候搬到了爱尔兰。2019年山火之后，他和妻子安妮离开了加利福尼亚。“我妻子说，我们需要搬到一个下雨的地方。”他们现在在科克郡巴尔的摩经营一家名为“阿尔及尔”的酒吧。希利亚德说，他现在尽量避开美国那些动荡事件。“我尽量不看新闻，因为我现在在这里，”他说。“但我每天都会被提醒，因为每个人都问我特朗普和那边的情况……我现在简直是西科克驻美国大使。” -- 获取面向董事会及更广泛决策层的全球洞察与专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》通讯，而《精选清单》则为你带来精心挑选的特写与见解。获取更多商业及更多领域内容，请在领英上关注我们。商业 迁移 特写 商业世界

readings.title: What Democrats are still getting wrong about voters
body: America, Actually What Democrats are still getting wrong about voters Sarah Longwell explains how Democrats could win 2026 — and still lose the bigger fight. by Cameron Peters and Astead Herndon Sep 30, 2026, 10:10 PM UTC Gift Congressional Democrats outside the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images With the 2026 midterm elections fast approaching, polling increasingly suggests that the GOP is in for a bad time. As the Iran war drives up inflation and fuel prices , Republicans are on the back foot not just in swing states like Michigan, but in redder parts of the map: Iowa, Texas, and maybe even Kansas , among others. (Not to mention Georgia and North Carolina .) It’s shaping up to be a Democratic wave, in other words, and a major repudiation of President Donald Trump. According to Sarah Longwell, the publisher of political news site the Bulwark, there’s a clear reason why this is the cycle that things seem to be falling apart for Trump, who has dodged scandals and bad poll numbers before. “The average person is often voting on instinctual things,” she explains, “and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially.” And for many voters right now, things are not okay materially. Longwell would know: She regularly speaks with voters for her podcast, The Focus Group , and she’s the author of the new book How to Eat an Elephant: One Voter at a Time . Longwell talked with Vox’s Astead Herndon for a special live recording of the America, Actually podcast at the Texas Tribune Festival earlier this month about why voters are both more and less complicated than punditry sometimes suggests, what the future holds for the Republican Party post-Trump, and the lesson Democrats need to learn to capitalize on their wins. Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Longwell, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel . One of the themes in the book is to talk to voters like real adults. What does that mean? There was a long period of time in our history where the artifice of politics was part of the performance of politics. You could give a good speech. You’d do a debate. Those are not the rules of politics in this communications environment anymore. Every single one of you, if you’re a Bulwark person, you interact with me. I am in your ear, and we’re having a conversation. We have a parasocial relationship. I walked in here and met a bunch of people, and they were like, “I feel like I know you.” And people want to feel like that about their political leaders now. And so they want to know what makes you tick. Are you a real person? And so the artifice of a debate on CNN is starting to feel really stupid, no offense to CNN. People demand more now. And a lot of it is just that artifice is falling away for voters. Donald Trump understood that as a person who had been in people’s living rooms as a performer. Democratic politicians still have not figured it out. One of the things that comes through in both the book and I think the work that we both do is how voters don’t always fit into those neat ideological boxes. I always tell the story about when I was at the Iowa caucuses, and I remember in 2019 in the Democratic primary, someone telling me they were stuck between Bernie [Sanders] and [former New York City Mayor Michael] Bloomberg, and asking, “How did you get there?” And what was the answer? I think the short answer was they liked a strong guy where they knew what he believed in. And they did not care which side of that coin that was, as long as it felt consistent and something they could put their hands around. If ideology is not the controlling paradigm for voters, how should we think about the different ways people are sorting themselves right now? My answer is genuinely not to sort them as much. This is the reason people say things like, “It’s the economy, stupid,” and then everybody gets bored with that answer, and they want to talk about 10 other things because they’re like, “Well, that’s so straightforward.” But I try in the book to say it really is about improving people’s material well-being and ensuring their safety. So you go back to: What are the most human things that people want? They want to be able to afford gas. They want a job. They want a job [where] they think that they can go up the ladder. They want their kids to get a good education. Then they want to be safe. They want to know that they’re safe in their community. They want to know they’re safe in the places that they go. And Donald Trump and Republicans really do understand: People vote with weird animal instincts. Now, I bet a lot of the people in this room are college-educated suburban voters, but the average voter in a general election is a 55-year-old white guy without a college degree. The average person is often voting on instinctual things, and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially — your cost of health care, and then for you to be safe. And so if you think about those base-level desires and then think about what Democrats spend most of their time talking about, you’re like, “Is that the thing that captures all these people?” When I watch Democrats as somebody who’s an immigrant into the Democratic ecosystem, there’s a lot of, like, “And you get a policy, and you get a policy, and you get a policy.” And I don’t really understand that because everybody needs cheaper gas. Everybody needs groceries that they can afford. And so talking about the things that unite us or that everybody needs, to me, is the secret sauce for how Democrats should think about policy. Three years ago, Democrats thought that being against January 6th was a thing that united everybody. There was a belief that pro-democracy arguments were going to unite people across ideology. Why did that fail in 2024? I’ve been thinking about this a lot as Trump gets terrible poll after terrible poll, and this is my point. The coup, all of the horrible things he said about women, all of the lawsuits — I mean, he told everybody an election was stolen. Why is he underwater right now? Because of gas prices, because of a war in Iran, because the negative personal consequences of his policies are hitting people. I know that it frustrates people. I’m so aware of the frustration where people are like, “Why are people so selfish? Why don’t they think about the bigger picture of democracy?” And one of the things I try not to do is magic words — consultant stuff, because a lot of consultants do that. They’re like, “Say freedom,” and “Say affordability.” There’s nothing to back it up. But the one magic word I do think that Democrats should start using is “America,” and swap it in for “democracy.” And the reason is, voters practice democracy in America by its individual things. They practice free speech. They like rule of law. They like checks and balances. So they like the elements of democracy, but they don’t think about them up here as democracy. And also the word democracy now is very polarized, right? Republicans think that Democrats are a threat to democracy because they stole the 2020 election. And Democrats think Republicans are a threat to democracy because they lied about the election being stolen and then tried to overturn the entire government. I think one side of that equation is more right than the other. But I think that’s why it didn’t work. I want to look ahead. Our show focuses on building a roadmap for American politics without Trump, and part of that question has been about Republicans. They have made themselves into a new kind of America First-esque party. But what does that mean without Trump at the center of it? When you’re in your focus groups, is it clear what values or principles Republicans believe in besides what Donald Trump says to them? Absolutely not. They don’t have anything. This is why I wrote the book. I wrote the book because we have 2026, we have 2028, and we have 2032. By 2032, there’s going to be a new census, and things are going to get worse for Democrats. Hear me on this. People are not grokking this yet. The map — people are leaving California for Texas, people are leaving New York for Florida, and it’s just going to get harder for Democrats to win if this same trajectory that we’re currently on holds. But there is a generational opportunity right now, and it’s why I desperately wanted to bring this book and get it out there. The Republican Party at this moment is as hollowed out as ... Donald Trump is going to leave it in shambles. There is no Trump heir who can do what Trump does, who has the longstanding parasocial relationship with voters where they give him this blank check that other people don’t get. But my concern is that 2026 will go really well and that Democrats will say, “See? It’s fine. Everybody likes us.” They don’t. This was the big mistake in 2022. The midterms were extrapolated [to signal] Biden’s re-election, and those were not the same thing. They are not the same thing. And again, the average voter is a 55-year-old white man without a college degree. And you can just hold that in your head and picture that guy and say, “Do we have candidates who can appeal to that guy?” I was being annoying when I was flying here, tweeting things, and there’s a new poll out for [Pennsylvania Gov.] Josh Shapiro. He is beating his Republican opponent by 21 points in the poll right now. This is the largest swing state in the country, and Democrats hate Josh Shapiro. Hate feels a little strong. I think the left doesn’t like Josh Shapiro. I don’t think that’s the whole party. That’s a good point. I’ll just say, as a slight Josh Shapiro stan, perhaps I feel more than most people’s antipathy to the idea of Josh Shapiro running. I get a lot of people just being like, “Absolutely not. He’s a corporate centrist. We would never consider him. And also he’s Jewish slash Zionist.” And a lot of this is Twitter discourse, but it feels like he doesn’t get the same buzz or interest, which seems insane to me when you’ve got somebody that popular in such a big, important state that Trump was able to win twice. The electoral argument for the Josh Shapiros of the world is clear. Twenty-one points in Pennsylvania at any rate is impressive, but let’s use him as an example, because I do think it speaks to where some Democrats have gone in the last couple years. The polling will tell you that the majority of Democrats want to see their party reshift its relationship with Israel and want to see things like an arms embargo. Polling would tell you that the majority of Democrats believe that they shouldn’t be taking corporate money, or that things like AIPAC money are bad. How does a Josh Shapiro — let’s use him as an avatar. … Is that compatible with where the Democratic base is right now, even if it’s clearly compatible with Pennsylvania? The way that you just said it doesn’t sound compatible. But I don’t think that it’s incompatible. This is a book about what the voters think, and the voters want a new relationship with Israel, hands down. Without question. They want America to reevaluate our relationship with Israel. And the next Democratic presidential candidate is going to have to do that. And I have a theory about this. I do think that the 2028 nominee is very likely to be a Jewish person who is highly critical of Israel, because I think that it helps to heal the deep divide right now on this issue within the Democratic Party. Now, do I think it’s more likely that that is the very handsome Jon Ossoff? I kind of do. But I just ... a big part of this book is, “Don’t you want to win? Don’t you guys want to win?” Like, do you want to win more than you want to be right about everything? ##段落
美国，实际上 民主党人仍然误解选民的地方 莎拉·朗韦尔解释了民主党人如何在2026年获胜——却仍输掉更大的战斗。 作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯和阿斯特德·赫恩登 2026年9月30日，晚上10:10 UTC 礼物 2026年5月21日，美国国会大厦外的国会民主党人。Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images 随着2026年中期选举迅速临近，民调越来越表明共和党将迎来艰难时期。由于伊朗战争推高通胀和燃油价格，共和党不仅在密歇根等摇摆州处于守势，在更偏红的地区也是如此：艾奥瓦州、得克萨斯州，甚至可能包括堪萨斯州等。（更不用说佐治亚州和北卡罗来纳州。）换句话说，这正在形成一场民主党浪潮，也是对唐纳德·特朗普总统的重大否定。根据政治新闻网站The Bulwark的出版人莎拉·朗韦尔的说法，对于此前曾躲过丑闻和糟糕民调的特朗普来说，这个周期之所以似乎开始崩解，有一个明确原因。“普通人往往凭本能投票，”她解释说，“而这些本能很大程度上是你那种动物性的欲望，希望物质生活一切安好。”而对当下许多选民来说，物质生活并不好。朗韦尔对此很了解：她定期为播客《焦点小组》与选民交谈，也是新书《如何吃下一头大象：一次一个选民》的作者。本月早些时候，朗韦尔在得克萨斯论坛节上，为Vox的《美国，实际上》播客特别现场录制，与Vox的阿斯特德·赫恩登交谈，讨论了为什么选民既比评论界有时暗示的更复杂，也比其暗示的更简单，共和党在特朗普之后将走向何方，以及民主党人需要吸取什么教训，才能把胜利转化为更大成果。以下是阿斯特德与朗韦尔对话的节选，为长度和清晰度作了编辑。完整节目还有更多内容，所以请在您获取播客的任何平台收听《美国，实际上》，或在Vox的YouTube频道观看。

##段落
书中一个主题是像对待真正的成年人一样与选民交谈。这是什么意思？在我们历史的很长一段时间里，政治的人为包装是政治表演的一部分。你可以发表一场好演讲。你可以参加一场辩论。在如今的传播环境中，这些已不再是政治规则。如果你们是The Bulwark的受众，你们每一个人都在与我互动。我在你耳边，我们在对话。我们有一种准社会关系。我走进这里，遇到一群人，他们说：“我觉得我认识你。”而人们现在希望对自己的政治领袖也有这种感觉。因此，他们想知道是什么让你运转。你是一个真实的人吗？所以，CNN上一场辩论的人为包装

##段落
开始让人觉得真的很愚蠢，无意冒犯CNN。人们现在要求更多。很大程度上只是因为，对选民来说，那些矫饰正在消退。唐纳德·特朗普明白这一点，因为他曾作为一个表演者进入过人们的客厅。民主党政治人物却还没搞明白。这本书里，以及我认为我们两人所做的工作中，都透露出一点：选民并不总是能被塞进那些整齐的意识形态盒子里。我总讲一个故事：我在艾奥瓦州党团会议现场时，记得2019年民主党初选期间，有人告诉我他们在伯尼[·桑德斯]和[前纽约市长迈克尔]布隆伯格之间难以抉择，我问：“你怎么会卡在这两个人之间？”答案是什么？我想简短的回答是，他们喜欢一个强硬的人，而且知道这个人相信什么。他们不在乎那是硬币的哪一面，只要感觉前后一致，是他们能抓得住的东西就行。如果意识形态不是选民的支配性范式，那我们现在该如何理解人们正在以不同方式给自己归类？我的回答是，真的不要那么急着给他们归类。这就是为什么人们会说“问题是经济，傻瓜”，然后所有人又对这个答案感到厌烦，想谈另外10件事，因为他们觉得：“嗯，那也太直白了。”但我在书里试图说明，这真的就是关乎改善人们的物质福祉并确保他们的安全。所以你还是得回到：人们想要的最人性化的东西是什么？他们希望能加得起油。他们想要一份工作。他们想要一份自己认为能沿着阶梯往上走的工作。他们想要孩子接受良好教育。然后他们想要安全。他们想知道自己在社区里是安全的。他们想知道自己去的地方是安全的。而唐纳德·特朗普和共和党人确实明白：人们投票时带着古怪的动物本能。现在，我敢打赌，这个房间里很多人都是受过大学教育的郊区选民，但大选中的普通选民是一个没有大学学位的55岁白人男性。普通人往往凭本能投票，而那些本能很大程度上是你动物性的欲望：希望物质上过得去——医疗费用别太高，然后希望自己安全。所以，如果你想想这些底层欲望，再想想民主党人大部分时间在谈什么，你就会想：“那东西能抓住所有这些选民吗？”当我以一个进入民主党生态系统的移民身份观察民主党人时，会看到很多类似“给你一项政策，给你一项政策，再给你一项政策”的东西。我不太理解这一点，因为每个人都需要更便宜的汽油。每个人都需要

## 买得起的生活必需品。所以，谈论那些把我们联结在一起的东西、那些每个人都需要的需求，对我来说，这就是民主党人思考政策时的秘诀。三年前，民主党人以为反对1月6日事件是团结所有人的事情。当时有一种信念，认为支持民主的论点能够跨越意识形态把人们团结起来。那为什么在2024年失败了？随着特朗普一个接一个糟糕的民调出来，我一直在思考这个问题，这就是我的观点。那场政变，他对女性说过的所有可怕的话，所有的诉讼——我是说，他告诉所有人选举被偷走了。为什么他现在民调处于水下？因为油价，因为伊朗的战争，因为他政策的负面个人后果正在冲击人们。我知道这让人们感到沮丧。我非常清楚那种挫败感，人们会说：“为什么人们这么自私？为什么他们不考虑民主这个更大的图景？”我尽量不做的一件事就是念咒语——那种顾问式的套路，因为很多顾问就是这么干的。他们会说“说自由”，“说可负担性”。背后什么支撑都没有。但我确实认为民主党人应该开始使用的一个咒语是“美国”，用它来替换“民主”。原因是，选民在美国是通过一件件具体的事情来实践民主的。他们实践言论自由。他们喜欢法治。他们喜欢制衡。所以他们喜欢民主的各个要素，但他们不会在脑子里把它们想成“民主”。而且“民主”这个词现在非常两极分化，对吧？共和党人认为民主党人是民主的威胁，因为他们偷走了2020年大选。民主党人认为共和党人是民主的威胁，因为他们谎称选举被偷走，然后试图推翻整个政府。我认为这个等式的一边比另一边更有道理。但我认为这就是为什么那套说法没有奏效。我想往前看。我们的节目聚焦于为没有特朗普的美国政治绘制路线图，而这个问题的一部分关乎共和党。他们已经把自己变成了一个新版的“美国优先”式政党。但如果没有特朗普作为核心，那意味着什么？当你在做焦点小组的时候，除了特朗普对他们说的话之外，共和党人相信什么价值观或原则，这一点清楚吗？完全不清楚。他们什么都没有。这就是我写这本书的原因。我写这本书是因为我们有2026年，我们有2028年，我们有2032年。到2032年，会有新的人口普查，情况对民主党人来说会变得更糟。听我说。人们还没有真正理解这一点。版图——人们在离开加州去得克萨斯，人们在离开纽约去佛罗里达，民主党人要赢得选举只会越来越难。

##段落
如果我们目前所处的这条轨迹保持不变，那就会赢。但眼下存在一个世代性的机会，这正是我迫切想要把这本书写出来并公之于众的原因。共和党此刻已经被掏空得……唐纳德·特朗普会把它弄得支离破碎。没有哪个特朗普的继承者能做特朗普所做的事，能拥有那种与选民长期建立的准社会关系——选民给他一张别人得不到的空白支票。但我担心的是，2026年会大获全胜，然后民主党人会说：“看吧？没事。大家都喜欢我们。”他们并不喜欢。这是2022年的大错。中期选举被外推为（预示）拜登连任，而这两者并不是一回事。它们不是一回事。再说一遍，普通选民是一个55岁、没有大学学位的白人男性。你可以在脑子里记住这一点，想象那个人的样子，然后问：“我们有能吸引那个人的候选人吗？”我坐飞机来这里的时候一直在发推，挺烦人的，而有一项关于[宾夕法尼亚州州长]乔什·夏皮罗的新民调出来了。他现在在民调中以21个百分点领先他的共和党对手。这是全国最大的摇摆州，而民主党人讨厌乔什·夏皮罗。讨厌这个词有点重。我觉得左翼不喜欢乔什·夏皮罗。我不认为那是整个党。这点说得好。我就说，作为一个稍微有点乔什·夏皮罗粉丝的人，也许我对乔什·夏皮罗参选这一想法的反感比大多数人更强。我遇到很多人就是那种态度：“绝对不行。他是个企业派中间派。我们绝不会考虑他。而且他还是犹太人，或者说犹太复国主义者。”这很多都是推特上的话语，但感觉他得不到同样的热度或关注，这在我看来简直疯了——你在一个如此庞大、如此重要、特朗普还能赢两次的州里，居然有这么一个受欢迎的人。为乔什·夏皮罗这类人辩护的选举论据很清楚。宾夕法尼亚州的21个百分点无论如何都很惊人，但我们拿他当例子吧，因为我确实认为这说明了部分民主党人过去几年走到了哪里。民调会告诉你，大多数民主党人希望看到本党重新调整与以色列的关系，希望看到武器禁运之类的事情。民调会告诉你，大多数民主党人认为他们不应该拿企业的钱，或者认为像AIPAC的钱这种东西是坏的。一个乔什·夏皮罗——我们就拿他当化身吧。……这跟民主党基本盘目前的立场相容吗，即便它显然跟宾夕法尼亚州相容？你刚才那样说，听起来并不相容。但我不认为它不相容。这是一本关于选民怎么想的书，而选民想要一种新的关系

##与以色列的关系，毫无疑问，绝对如此。他们希望美国重新审视我们与以色列的关系。而下一任民主党总统候选人将不得不这样做。对此我有一个理论。我确实认为，2028年的提名人很可能是一位对以色列持强烈批评态度的犹太人，因为我认为这有助于弥合当前民主党内部在这个问题上的深刻分歧。那么，我认为那个人更有可能是那位非常英俊的乔恩·奥索夫吗？我确实有点这么认为。但我只是……这本书的很大一部分是，“你们不想赢吗？你们难道不想赢吗？”就像，你们想赢的欲望，是否超过了想在一切事情上都正确的欲望？查看更多：美国、2026年中期选举、播客、政治、视频。特朗普试图让汉堡更便宜。结果适得其反，而且非常惨烈。用最新的Vox填字游戏让大脑休息一下。这个免费、略带野性的爱好将帮你戒掉末日刷屏。美国建造最快和最慢的城市之间令人震惊的差距。所有素食餐厅都去哪儿了？邮箱（必填）注册。提交你的邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA以及谷歌隐私政策和服务条款保护。广告商内容来自：这是原生广告的标题。

readings.title: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
body: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
What separates the very best in the world from the remaining 7 billion of us?

Exceptional talent often looks like an act of revolution — a person doing something in a way no one has ever done it before — but many revolutionary talents are actually built on a foundation of evolutionary tweaks. These tweaks develop over time, often compensating for weaknesses and anxieties that might derail a lesser talent.
For all his brilliance, though, Messi is famously anxious. For several years, he habitually vomited on the field before big matches.

Take the world’s best soccer player, an Argentinean named Lionel Messi. Messi has won more Ballon d’Or trophies, awarded to the best soccer player of the year, than any other player. He has scored more goals in a calendar year than any other living player, is the top all-time scorer in Spain’s La Liga, and has the highest goal ratio in the sport today, scoring almost once every match.

For all his brilliance, though, he’s famously anxious. For several years, Messi habitually vomited on the field before big matches. After a string of disappointing national-team losses, another former Argentinean giant of the game, the late Diego Maradona, uncharitably criticized Messi by suggesting that it was “useless trying to make a leader out of a man who goes to the toilet twenty times before a game.”

Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, and many of the world’s best grapple with anxiety precisely because they expect so much from themselves. But Messi hasn’t allowed his anxiety to diminish his brilliance because he’s mastered a coping mechanism that also doubles as the secret behind his tactical brilliance.
Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Second, he scopes out the opposition.

A soccer match runs for 90 minutes (plus a few minutes for “injury time”), and most players are active in the game from the first minute. As soon as the whistle blows, they implore their teammates to pass the ball and pursue the tactics their coaches laid out before the game.

But Messi is famous for not playing the game during its opening minutes. This is his evolutionary tweak, which developed as he played the game at progressively higher levels. For the opening minutes, Messi ambles back and forth near the middle of the field and almost never engages with his teammates. Whereas other players run and sometimes sprint, Messi spends much of his time walking, rarely breaking into more than a slow jog.

Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Easing into the game is Messi’s way of ensuring he’s fully engaged for the remainder of the game. His on-field vomiting has resolved itself, in part perhaps because he’s found a more effective way to calm his nerves. Second, he spends this time scoping out the opposition. His legs move slowly, but his eyes dart from player to player, assessing his opponents’ strengths, weaknesses, and tactics, and monitoring his own team’s movement with and around the ball. Messi is less valuable to his team early in the game, but this tactical pause elevates his value for the remaining 95 percent of the game.

If you split soccer game play into “preparatory” and “engaged” components, Messi leans heavily on preparation. During one classic game between Messi’s Barcelona and archrivals Real Madrid, in 2017, Messi ran for just four minutes and walked for more than eighty of the game’s ninety minutes. When he was engaged, though, he was dynamic, creating nine chances, scoring one goal, and feeding the ball to a teammate who scored another goal.
As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act.

That pattern isn’t unusual for Messi, and it’s often in the biggest games that he accentuates his in-game preparation. That preparation also explains his ability to find himself in the right place at the right time, over and over. Though his positional play appears otherworldly, it isn’t a miracle; it’s that he’s learned, minute by minute, that a particular defender leaves a particular square of pitch uncovered or that two midfielders leave a small corner of the pitch open when they gravitate to the middle of the field.
The lesson for the rest of us is clear: When you’re anxious, whether in athletics or in life more broadly, pause. Slow down . Prepare.

As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act. Judson Brewer, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist, has spent much of his career thinking about how to do nothing.
About fifteen years ago, Brewer developed a mindfulness-based treatment for addiction.
His approach instructs addicts to resist the waves of anxiety during moments of craving by following the four steps of an approach that goes by the acronym RAIN:
I nvestigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., “What is happening in my body now?”)
N ote what is happening from moment to moment.

Brewer has said that his approach was inspired by clinical psychologist Tara Brach’s . To test the approach, Brewer worked with smokers who were struggling to quit. Nicotine addiction is notoriously stubborn — more so than many harder drugs that produce stronger immediate responses in users.

Before unleashing the program on smokers, Brewer wanted to test the system on himself. The problem was “I was a nonsmoker,” Brewer wrote, “who needed to be able to relate to patients who felt as though their heads were going to explode unless they smoked.”

Nicotine has a half-life of around two hours, so to begin, smokers need to resist the urge to light up for two hours at a time. Brewer reasoned that smokers who could last two hours without a cigarette would cultivate new nonsmoking habits, extending those stretches till they no longer felt the urge to smoke at all.

He simulated these periods of resistance by learning to meditate for two-hour stretches without moving. During moments of restlessness, he followed the RAIN steps — recognize, allow, investigate, note — and if he moved his body, the clock would reset, and he’d have to start again.

This might sound easy, but two hours is a long time to sit still without entertainment. “Surprisingly it wasn’t the physical pain of not shifting for a long time that got me,” Brewer wrote. “It was the restlessness … Those cravings shouted, ‘Get up!’ ”
Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean.

For many months, Brewer would get close, then restlessness would defeat him. “Then one day,” he wrote, “I did it. I sat for the full two hours … Each subsequent sit got easier and easier because I had the confidence that it could be done. And I knew that my patients could quit smoking. They simply needed the proper tools.”

Brewer was right. His patients had been stuck, incapable of quitting one of the most addictive substances on earth. But when he ran study after study, pitting his RAIN mindfulness method against the most effective addiction treatment approaches of the day, his approach was more than twice as effective.

Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean. They were more than five times as likely to have shaken their addictions using an approach that essentially taught them to pause at the moment their bodies were most urgently driving them to act.

Of the four steps in Brewer’s RAIN approach, the second — allowing — is perhaps the most critical. Allowing an experience to wash over you sounds disarmingly easy because it doesn’t require you to do anything. But that’s exactly the point. It’s difficult because you’re forced to do nothing despite the urge to act.

##段落
以世界上最优秀的足球运动员、阿根廷人利昂内尔·梅西为例。梅西获得的金球奖——颁发给年度最佳足球运动员的奖项——比任何其他球员都多。他在一个自然年内的进球数超过任何在世球员，是西班牙甲级联赛的历史最佳射手，并且拥有当今足坛最高的进球率，几乎每场比赛攻入一球。
##段落
然而，尽管他才华横溢，他却以焦虑著称。有好几年，梅西在重大比赛前会习惯性地在球场上呕吐。在一连串令人失望的国家队失利之后，另一位阿根廷足球巨人、已故的迭戈·马拉多纳毫不留情地批评梅西，暗示“试图把一个赛前要上二十次厕所的人培养成领袖是徒劳的”。
##段落
天赋异禀并不能让你对焦虑免疫，世界上许多最优秀的人恰恰因为对自己期望过高而与焦虑搏斗。但梅西没有让焦虑削弱他的光芒，因为他掌握了一种应对机制，而这一机制同时也是他战术天赋背后的秘密。
##段落
梅西在开场几分钟里做两件事。第一，他让自己平静下来。第二，他观察对手。

一场足球比赛持续90分钟（外加几分钟“伤停补时”），大多数球员从第一分钟起就积极参与比赛。哨声一响，他们就催促队友传球，执行教练赛前布置的战术。
##段落
但梅西以在开场阶段不参与比赛而闻名。这就是他的渐进式微调，随着他在越来越高的水平上踢球而逐渐形成。在开场几分钟里，梅西在球场中场附近来回踱步，几乎从不与队友互动。其他球员奔跑甚至冲刺时，梅西大部分时间都在走路，很少加速到超过慢跑的节奏。

##For all the benefits of pausing and preparing, though, sometimes the main event doesn’t go to plan. readings.title: Is Italy the new tax haven for the global rich?
body: 22 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Italy has already been attacked by the French Government for using tax incentives to lure wealthy French and other international residents away, but with the war in the Middle East hurting the Gulf states, Italy has become an even more attractive location for the rich. Tax wasn't the main reason for leaving France, Robert insists over a café crème at Charles de Gaulle airport. It was the beauty of Italy, the bella vita  (the beautiful/good life), the art and the music. But for the Frenchman, buying a house in Rome and becoming an Italian tax resident was a very nice part of the package offered by the country, where high net worth individuals can pay a fixed annual tax on all foreign income – regardless of amount – and enjoy a series of other exemptions.  Robert, who describes himself as only "moderately wealthy", moved to Italy eight years ago after a career in computers which ended with him selling his company. Robert, not his real name, may not be among the French billionaires who have fled the French taxman for Italy, but the advantages to him are clear.   If he'd been buying a house in France, he would have had to pay what the French call frais de notaire (solicitor's fees) most of which goes to the government (much like Stamp Duty in the UK or Real Estate Transfer Taxes in the US). In Italy there's an exemption for the prima casa , the first house you buy. In France, President Macron transformed France's Impot sur la Fortune  (wealth tax) into an Impot sur la Fortune Immobilière  (real estate wealth tax) so stock market investments, for example, are no longer affected but "if you have ten million dollars' worth of property, this tax is very painful indeed," says Robert. Again, there's nothing like that in Italy.  In France you also have to pay a property tax ( taxe foncière or land tax). "We don't have that here for the prima casa (first home)," says Robert, although he notes "there is a high charge for refuse collection". The best thing as far as he is concerned is that there is no inheritance tax on property you own in Italy up to €1 million ($1.1 million) and it's only 4% beyond that threshold. In France the tax-free limit is much lower – €100,000 ($110,000) – and beyond that it's a sliding scale up to a top rate of 45%. But it's for the seriously rich that Italy starts to look like a fiscal paradise. "I have friends who have moved here for tax reasons and others who are thinking about it," Robert tells me. "For people who really pay a lot of tax, Italy is very attractive because of it's "flat tax". In Italy, the taxman fixes an upper limit of tax that can be levied on income. However much you earn, you never pay more than that. The upper limit is now €300,000 ($353,000). Although not long ago it was €100,000 before rising to €200,000. If you're paying a million euros of income tax a year in France, Italy is very tempting. As for US citizens, Americans are always taxable on worldwide income, so moving to Italy would not help their tax bill. Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe – Peter Ferrigno Robert tells me that he has two rich French friends who have moved to Italy in the past few months, but they came from the UK. They were both working in finance in the City of London and were keen to move to a place where the fiscal regime was as sympathetic to them as the one Britain had before it changed the rules for wealthy foreign residents.  "Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe. And it means you get tax certainty and clarity, within the heart of Europe, rather than having to go a long way," says Peter Ferrigno, director of tax services at wealth migration specialists Henley & Partners. "We have meetings with people every week who would like to leave France," says Paris-based tax lawyer Jerome Barre. "They are unhappy about the tax situation now and they are worried that it will become harsher in the future. People are not confident with the political climate. Taxes are changing a lot, almost every year. People are frightened that after the election of the new president in 2027, things could become harder than today," he says. At this stage though it's more "questions from entrepreneurs and wealthy people who are wondering if they would like to move or not move rather than people actually moving," Jerome Barre explains. "Relocation requires full commitment and careful structuring," he stresses. He adds that for business-owners  " they need to change the seat of the company. They are subject in France to an exit tax." If many wealthy French people are at the "thinking-about-moving" stage, the question is being felt even more acutely in the United Arab Emirates. It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE – Peter Ferrigno But giving up on Dubai's zero-tax regime will be very difficult for many. "When you are in a country where you do not pay any tax, it's very difficult to come back to a country where you have to pay a lot. Especially for those used to spending a lot of money. The net in your pocket is very different, says Barre. And, he adds, people who have grown used to the zero-tax life "are not used to administrative formalities anymore – tax returns, documents – so it's not easy." More like this: • Dubai's tourism industry reels from 'brutal' impact of war • Why more Americans are now moving to Ireland • Is New York's cannabis business really flying high? "It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE," says Henley & Partners' Peter Ferrigno. "But I think it's far too early for people to wholesale uproot their life when it involves work, family, etc. The vast majority of people in the UAE are still regular people doing regular jobs, even most of the millionaires are millionaires because they are doing well paid jobs rather than being asset owners. If the war is relatively short, they will remain. If it drags on, then people will inevitably look elsewhere, or relocate the family and work remotely until it's safer. If you're in the UAE for work, there aren't likely to be that many equivalent roles in Italy," he says. However, it is likely that the war in the Middle East will dissuade many rich Europeans who would have otherwise moved there from re-locating to the UAE. Last year, Dubai was the number one destination by far for migrating millionaires, according to Henley & Partners. That number is bound to tumble in 2026, and with its attractive offer for the very wealthy, as well as its reputation for  la dolce vita  of course, it may well be Italy that benefits. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights.  For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . ##段落
2026年4月22日 分享 保存 在谷歌上添加为首选 约翰·劳伦森 意大利已经因利用税收优惠吸引富有的法国人和其他国际居民而遭到法国政府的抨击，但随着中东战争对海湾国家的冲击，意大利对富人来说变得更具吸引力。罗伯特在戴高乐机场喝着一杯咖啡奶油时坚称，税收并不是他离开法国的主要原因。真正的原因是意大利的美景、美好的生活、艺术和音乐。但对这位法国人来说，在罗马买房并成为意大利税务居民，是这个国家所提供的一揽子方案中非常美好的一部分——在意大利，高净值个人可以就所有海外收入缴纳固定的年度税额，无论金额多少，并享受一系列其他豁免。罗伯特自称只是"中等富裕"，八年前在计算机行业结束职业生涯并卖掉公司后搬到了意大利。罗伯特并非他的真名，他可能不属于那些为逃避法国税务而逃往意大利的法国亿万富翁之列，但对他来说好处是显而易见的。如果他是在法国买房，就必须支付法国人所说的"公证费"，其中大部分归政府所有（类似于英国的印花税或美国的房地产转让税）。而在意大利，购买第一套住房可以享受豁免。在法国，马克龙总统将法国的财富税改为房地产财富税，因此股票市场投资等不再受影响，但罗伯特说："如果你有价值一千万美元的房产，这项税确实非常痛苦。"而在意大利，完全没有这样的税。在法国，你还必须缴纳房产税。罗伯特说："我们这里对第一套住房不征收这个税"，不过他指出"垃圾收集费很高"。在他看来，最好的一点是，你在意大利拥有的房产价值不超过100万欧元（约110万美元）时无需缴纳遗产税，超过该门槛也只需缴纳4%。而在法国，免税上限要低得多——仅为10万欧元（约11万美元）——超过部分则按累进税率计算，最高可达45%。但正是对真正的富豪而言，意大利才开始看起来像是一个税收天堂。罗伯特告诉我："我有朋友因税收原因搬到了这里，还有其他人在考虑这样做。对于真正缴纳大量税款的人来说，意大利非常有吸引力，因为它有'单一税'。"在意大利，税务部门对收入征税设定了上限。无论你赚多少，缴纳的税款都不会超过这个上限。目前的上限是30万欧元（约35.3万美元）。尽管

##段落
不久前还是10万欧元，后来涨到了20万欧元。如果你在法国每年缴纳100万欧元的所得税，意大利就非常诱人了。至于美国公民，美国人始终需要就全球收入纳税，所以搬到意大利并不会减轻他们的税负。即便税率定在30万欧元，对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，意大利的单一税率与欧洲其他任何地方相比仍然很低——彼得·费里尼奥告诉我，他有两位富有的法国朋友在过去几个月里搬到了意大利，但他们是从英国过去的。这两人此前都在伦敦金融城从事金融工作，他们急切地想要搬到一个财税制度对他们友善的地方，就像英国在修改针对富裕外国居民的规定之前那样。

##段落
“即便税率定在30万欧元，对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，意大利的单一税率与欧洲其他任何地方相比仍然很低。而且这意味着你能在欧洲腹地获得税收的确定性和透明度，而不必远走他乡，”财富移民专业机构Henley & Partners的税务服务总监彼得·费里尼奥表示。“我们每周都会与想要离开法国的人会面，”巴黎税务律师杰罗姆·巴雷说。“他们对当前的税收状况感到不满，并且担心未来会变得更加严苛。人们对政治气候缺乏信心。税收变化很大，几乎每年都在变。人们担心2027年新总统当选后，情况可能会比现在更糟，”他说。不过，杰罗姆·巴雷解释说，在现阶段，更多的是“企业家和富人提出疑问，思考自己到底要不要搬走，而非真正付诸行动”。“搬迁需要全身心的投入和精心的规划，”他强调。他还补充说，对于企业主而言，“他们需要变更公司的注册地。在法国，他们需要缴纳退出税。”

##段落
如果说许多法国富人还处于“考虑搬迁”的阶段，那么在阿联酋，这个问题感受得更为强烈。彼得·费里尼奥说，很多人重新考虑阿联酋是不可避免的。但对许多人来说，放弃迪拜的零税制将非常困难。“当你身处一个不用缴任何税的国家，再回到一个需要缴纳大量税款的国家，是非常困难的。尤其是对那些习惯了高消费的人来说。到手的净收入差别非常大，”巴雷说。他还补充说，那些已经习惯了零税生活的人“不再习惯行政手续——纳税申报、文件——所以并不容易。”更多类似内容：• 迪拜旅游业遭受战争的“残酷”冲击 • 为什么越来越多美国人正在移居爱尔兰 • 纽约的大麻生意真的在腾飞吗

##段落
“很多人会重新考虑阿联酋，这是不可避免的，”Henley & Partners的彼得·费里尼奥表示。“但我认为，现在就让人彻底连根拔起、抛弃工作、家庭等一切，还为时过早。阿联酋的绝大多数人仍然是做着普通工作的普通人，即便是大多数百万富翁，他们之所以是百万富翁，也是因为从事高薪工作，而不是因为拥有资产。如果战争相对短暂，他们会留下来。如果战争拖下去，人们必然会另寻他处，或者把家人安置到别处、自己远程工作，直到局势更安全。如果你在阿联酋是为了工作，意大利不太可能有那么多对等的职位，”他说。然而，中东战争很可能会让许多原本会迁往那里的富裕欧洲人打消移居阿联酋的念头。根据Henley & Partners的数据，去年迪拜是迄今为止 migrating millionaires 的首选目的地。这一数字在2026年势必大幅下滑，而凭借其对超级富豪的吸引力，当然还有“甜蜜生活”的声誉，受益的很可能正是意大利。——欲获取面向董事会及更广泛决策层的全球洞察与专家分析，请订阅《World of Business》通讯，而《The Essential List》则精选推送专题与洞察。欲了解更多商业及更多领域内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业 国际商业 专题 《World of Business》

readings.title: How to make an artificial star - with lasers
body: 20 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Richard Fisher For the first time in its history, the Very Large Telescope in Chile is operating with up to seven lasers that fire up into the atmosphere. But why do astronomers need them? If you happened to be wandering Chile's Atacama Desert in the middle of the night, you might encounter an extraordinary scene: the sight of enormous lasers piercing the sky. From a distance, you'd see them emerging from a sci-fi structure on a mountain top, like the lair of an evil villain.   Closer up, though, you'd discover the source is actually a telescope – a particularly big one – made up of several buildings. Inside, teams of astronomers on the night shift would be positioning the lasers to create an "artificial star" at the edge of Earth's atmosphere. If you were passing by this evening, you might catch them firing four lasers from four separate structures on the mountain-top at the same time – which would be a first.  This is the Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal – operated by the European Southern Observatory (Eso) – which the BBC recently visited . In late 2025, engineers there finished installing the last of a series of powerful new lasers to help astronomers peer into the cosmos with greater fidelity, taking the total number to seven. But why do telescopes need such lasers in the first place?  The idea for using lasers in astronomy can be traced back to the Cold War, when the US military developed technology to track Soviet satellites. Astronomers eventually realised that similar techniques would help improve their observations from the ground. Why? Telescopes on Earth's surface face a barrier that space telescopes do not: the atmosphere. The gases clinging to our planet distort starlight before it reaches a ground telescope's mirror. Atmospheric conditions continually change too.   "We are protected by our atmosphere, which is fantastic. But as an astronomer it is horrible, because the atmosphere basically messes with the sharpness of the light coming from stars and galaxies," says astronomer Amelia Bayo, a project scientist with Eso who advises on how to get the most from the VLT's instruments . "If you don't compensate for the atmosphere, your star is going to be jumping in different places of your detector and you will end up with a blurred image." Our atmosphere is sodium-rich. It offers a canvas where we can put the star anywhere we want – Amelia Bayo To get around this problem, astronomers apply an approach called " adaptive optics ". "The implementation is hard, but the idea is super simple," explains Bayo. After the distorted light strikes the telescope's primary mirror, it reflects to another smaller mirror that can deform to essentially match, and correct, the atmospheric distortion.  In the VLT, one of these adaptive mirrors contains piezoelectric materials – ones which can generate an electric charge – that can change shape at "crazy speeds", says Bayo. The mirror is also suspended inside a magnetic field . "It's stupidly cool. It is basically floating," she adds. For adaptive optics to work, though, astronomers need a star as a reference point – a fixed point in the sky. And crucially, it needs to be bright. Why? "Imagine that you're listening to a song, and you want to get the melody," explains Bayo. "If the volume is low; if there's more noise, or you only hear high or low pitch, then you may not be able to tell which song it is." It's the same with stars; a bright star provides more information to help correct the atmospheric distortion. Sometimes it's possible to use natural stars, but when astronomers look at a part of the sky without any suitably bright ones, they turn to lasers instead.  Firing lasers in the direction they are looking excites a sodium-rich layer in the atmosphere, around 90km (56 miles) above the ground. These sodium atoms will then emit photons that the mirrors back at the telescope can catch . In short, an artificial star. "Our atmosphere is sodium-rich. It offers a canvas where we can put the star anywhere we want," says Bayo. The lasers now installed at the VLT are state-of-the-art. Bayo remembers the previous generation were difficult to calibrate, requiring toxic liquid dyes, and days of engineering work to ensure stability. "Before it almost looked like you had a laser pointer you were holding in your shaking hand, and now you have a perfect stable device that launches a laser that is way more powerful." Today, the astronomers simply press a button to launch their laser, and it stays fixed in place all night. After upgrades in 2016, one of the four 8.2m-long (27ft) telescopes of the VLT (Yepun) gained the ability to fire four lasers simultaneously , which allows astronomers to correct atmospheric disturbance over a wider field of view. Each laser delivers 22 watts of power – about 4,000 times the maximum allowed for a laser pointer – in a 30cm-wide (12in) diameter beam. As of 2026, the four main telescopes of the VLT (Antu, Kueyen, Melipal and Yepun) can now also combine forces – in an act of astronomical Power Rangers – to fire lasers at the same time, assembling into a single, giant "virtual" telescope with a wider field of view. By working together, the four big mirrors in each of those four telescopes can capture details many times sharper than one alone.  The VLT has been responsible for some of the most significant astronomical discoveries of the 21st Century, including the first image of an extrasolar planet (one that lives outside of our Solar System), and the positions of individual stars moving around the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way's centre . More like this: •  This huge telescope in Chile could reveal alien life •  The hotel where astronomers live like James Bond spies •  The light disturbing a dark zone full of telescopes One final question you might wonder: what happens if a plane passes over? After all, even the smallest laser pointers pose a risk of dazzling pilots .  "Planes can of course pass above the observatory, but we have a safety mechanism," explains astronomer Itziar de Gregorio Monsalvo, Eso's representative in Chile. "If the planes cross near where we are observing, automatically the lasers switch off." So, that means if you wanted to see a very large telescope firing its very large lasers in the Atacama, you'd probably have to approach on the ground. But if you did, you'd encounter a scene rarely encountered in day-to-day life: a telescope lighting up an artificial star on the edge of our planet's atmosphere.  -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . ##段落
20小时前 分享 保存 在Google上添加为首选 理查德·费舍尔 智利的甚大望远镜在其历史上首次同时使用多达七束激光射向大气层。但天文学家为什么需要它们？如果你碰巧在半夜漫步智利的阿塔卡马沙漠，你可能会遇到一幕非凡的景象：巨大的激光束刺破夜空。从远处看，它们从山顶上一座科幻般的建筑中射出，就像邪恶反派的老巢。但走近一看，你会发现源头其实是一台望远镜——一台特别巨大的望远镜——由几座建筑组成。在里面，值夜班的天文学家团队会调整激光的位置，在地球大气层边缘制造出一颗“人造星”。如果你今晚路过，可能会看到他们同时从山顶上四个独立结构中射出四束激光——这将是史上首次。

##段落
这就是位于帕瑞纳的甚大望远镜（VLT）——由欧洲南方天文台（Eso）运营——BBC最近造访了这里。2025年底，那里的工程师完成了最后一批强大新激光器的安装，帮助天文学家以更高的保真度窥探宇宙，使激光总数达到七束。但望远镜为什么首先需要这样的激光呢？在天文学中使用激光的想法可以追溯到冷战时期，当时美国军方开发了追踪苏联卫星的技术。天文学家最终意识到，类似的技术有助于改善地面观测。为什么？地球表面的望远镜面临着一个太空望远镜所没有的障碍：大气层。附着在地球上的气体在星光到达地面望远镜的镜面之前就会使其扭曲。大气条件也在不断变化。

##段落
“我们受到大气层的保护，这非常好。但作为天文学家，这很糟糕，因为大气层基本上会扰乱来自恒星和星系的光的锐度，”天文学家阿梅莉亚·巴约说，她是Eso的项目科学家，就如何最大限度地发挥VLT仪器的性能提供建议。“如果你不对大气层进行补偿，你的恒星就会在探测器上的不同位置跳动，最终你会得到一张模糊的图像。”我们的大气层富含钠。它提供了一块画布，我们可以把星星放在任何我们想要的位置——阿梅莉亚·巴约 为了解决这个问题，天文学家采用了一种叫做“自适应光学”的方法。“实施起来很难，但想法超级简单，”巴约解释说。扭曲的光线击中望远镜的主镜后，会反射到另一个更小的镜面上，这个镜面可以变形，基本上就是匹配并校正大气的扭曲。在

##段落
VLT 的自适应反射镜之一含有压电材料——这种材料能够产生电荷——Bayo 表示，它能够以“疯狂的速度”改变形状。这面镜子还悬浮在一个磁场之中。“这酷得离谱。它基本上就是悬浮着的，”她补充道。不过，要让自适应光学系统发挥作用，天文学家需要一颗恒星作为参考点——天空中的一个固定点。而且至关重要的是，它必须足够明亮。为什么？“想象你在听一首歌，你想听出旋律，”Bayo 解释道。“如果音量很低；如果噪音更多，或者你只听到高音或低音，那你可能就分辨不出这是哪首歌了。”恒星也是如此；一颗明亮的恒星能提供更多信息，帮助校正大气畸变。有时可以使用自然恒星，但当天文学家观测的天空区域没有足够明亮的恒星时，他们就会转而使用激光。朝他们观测的方向发射激光，会激发大气中约 90 公里（56 英里）高处富含钠的层。这些钠原子随后会发射光子，望远镜上的反射镜便能捕捉到这些光子。简而言之，就是一颗人造恒星。“我们的大气层富含钠。它提供了一块画布，我们可以把恒星放在任何想要的位置，”Bayo 说。如今安装在 VLT 上的激光器是最先进的。Bayo 记得上一代激光器难以校准，需要使用有毒的液体染料，还要花数天工程工作来确保稳定性。“以前几乎就像你手里拿着一支激光笔，而手在发抖，现在你拥有了一台完美的稳定设备，发射出的激光要强大得多。”如今，天文学家只需按下一个按钮就能发射激光，而且它会整夜固定在那里。经过 2016 年的升级，VLT 四台 8.2 米长（27 英尺）望远镜之一（Yepun）获得了同时发射四束激光的能力，这使天文学家能够在更宽广的视场上校正大气扰动。每束激光以 30 厘米宽（12 英寸）的光束直径输出 22 瓦功率——约为激光笔最大允许功率的 4,000 倍。截至 2026 年，VLT 的四台主望远镜（Antu、Kueyen、Melipal 和 Yepun）现在还能合力——上演一场天文版“恐龙战队”——同时发射激光，组合成一台视场更宽广的单一巨型“虚拟”望远镜。通过协同工作，这四台望远镜中每一台里的四面大反射镜所能捕捉到的细节，比单独一台清晰许多倍。VLT 促成了 21 世纪一些最重要的天文发现，包括首张系外行星（位于我们太阳系之外的行星）图像，以及单颗恒星的位置 m

##段落
在银河系中心的超大质量黑洞周围移动。更多类似内容：• 智利的这座巨型望远镜可能揭示外星生命 • 天文学家像詹姆斯·邦德间谍一样生活的酒店 • 扰乱布满望远镜的暗区的光

##段落
你可能会想最后一个问题：如果有飞机从上方飞过会怎样？毕竟，即使是最小的激光笔也有让飞行员目眩的风险。“飞机当然可以从天文台上方飞过，但我们有安全机制，”天文学家、ESO驻智利代表伊齐亚尔·德·格雷戈里奥·蒙萨尔沃解释道。“如果飞机穿过我们正在观测的区域附近，激光会自动关闭。”所以，这意味着如果你想看到一台甚大望远镜在阿塔卡马发射其巨大的激光，你大概得从地面靠近。但如果你真这么做了，你会遇到日常生活中难得一见的场景：一台望远镜在地球大气层边缘点亮一颗人造星。

Matt Burkhartt/Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . Today’s newsletter is a heavy one — so please feel free to skip it if you need to. But as the uproar over an alarming rape allegation at Cornell University from 2024 keeps building, I wanted to take a minute to look at the facts of the case and the wider scourge of campus sexual assault. (We’ll get into that second topic in just a minute.) You’ve probably read about the case on social media, but if not, let me bring you up to speed. A former Cornell undergraduate student, identified as Jane Doe in a civil lawsuit filed earlier this month, alleges that seven men pressured her into drinking and snorting large amounts of ketamine, an anesthetic that can cause dissociation, before raping her at a campus fraternity house. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. At the time, she reported the incident to campus police — but her lawsuit alleges the men were never adequately investigated. Instead, the case was handled through Cornell’s administrative disciplinary system, which meted out noncriminal punishments, such as suspensions and expulsions, and permanently shuttered the fraternity house. The case and its handling have horrified observers online and in Ithaca , New York, where Cornell is located. In response to that uproar, the Tompkins County district attorney announced on Monday that he was reopening his office’s investigation. A nine-page statement further explained why the DA’s office didn’t file criminal charges two years ago: At the time, the statement says, the woman did not allege that she was incapacitated or that the encounter was nonconsensual. For many online, however, that explanation only prompted more questions, such as: Was Jane Doe ever interviewed by a specialist trained to speak to survivors? And what prompted her to go to police in the first place, if she believed the encounter was consensual? The reopened investigation will take time, but should provide some answers. Sexual assault remains appallingly common on college campuses. When I taught an undergraduate writing class in 2024, I assigned my students a personal essay and encouraged them to choose a topic they found weighty or meaningful. In a class of 11 women, two wrote about being assaulted at school. That proportion surprised and horrified me, though it shouldn’t have. Surveys have consistently estimated that roughly one in five undergraduate women experiences some form of sexual assault or nonconsensual contact during college. Awareness around the issue has grown over the past decade or so, particularly in light of the Me Too movement and after a string of high-profile cases in the mid-2010s. But progress has been more complicated. First, it’s difficult to know if the situation is improving or worsening, because the data around campus sexual assault is really limited . Federal law has historically required that universities disclose only the incidents reported through official channels — a small minority of all cases. In 2022, Congress enacted a requirement directing colleges and universities to begin conducting more comprehensive surveys on campus sexual assault every two years. That would have helped measure the true scope of the problem — arguably, a prerequisite for designing and tracking potential interventions. But the Biden administration never set up that survey , and President Donald Trump has, if anything, rolled back college sexual assault protections and slow-walked Title IX investigations related to sexual harassment and violence. Just Monday, in fact, Trump’s Department of Education formally rescinded Biden-era rules designed to better hold schools accountable for sexual assault. The department will now revert to rules put in place during Trump’s first term, which defined sexual harassment more narrowly and gave schools more latitude over how they handle allegations. It’s an amazing irony, really, that those rollbacks were formalized on the same day that prosecutors reopened the Cornell case. If anything, the outrage over that investigation shows that people want institutions to take sexual assault more seriously. ➨ Make art a little more personal. The average museumgoer looks at any one piece of art for only 27 seconds — maybe because it’s daunting to spend any more time on the task of Serious Art Appreciation. Instead of laboring to interpret a piece the “right” way, try relating it to your personal experience and other cultural objects you know well. This is also a correct and valid way to look at art! As one artist told Vox, “I don’t need the viewer of my paintings to know exactly what I meant…it’s more about an openness to a conversation.” Did you know …that the sun’s magnetic north and south poles reverse roughly every 11 years ? It generally doesn’t have much of an impact on Earth, though it can make the auroras more visible. Today’s trivia: The civil rights activist Ruby Bridges became famous at age 6 for doing what? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: We asked you for the name of the unrequited love interest in Victor Hugo’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame . That would be Esmeralda, whose fate was way darker in the 1831 novel than in the Disney movie version. readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 社交媒体平台曾经是朋友之间交流的工具——如今许多平台已日益成为短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，从而提升广告收入。但消费者是否已经开始反弹？

奥蕾莉亚给自己冲了杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近她美丽的花园里，打开Instagram“放松一下”。首先映入眼帘的是：“一个我很喜欢的做室内设计的人。他现在在威尼斯。”她对室内设计很感兴趣，甚至刚在手臂上纹了两幅19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的鸟类画作。她继续往下滑。两只小猫在打架。“我喜欢动物，所以推送给我很多动物。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点了香蕉，它就给你香蕉。”还有广告——虽然看起来和其他帖子一模一样——推销扫地机器人、减肥方案和床品（带有莫里斯风格的设计）。但没有朋友。她在Instagram上有198个好友，但她说“完全变了。我几乎看不到任何朋友的帖子了。”她自己也基本放弃了发帖。“反正我觉得也没人看得到了。”

尽管Instagram、尤其是Facebook上仍有忠实的社交型业余发帖者，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览不认识的人制作的专业内容，这一趋势在年轻用户中更为明显。16岁的基利安正在接受职业培训，将来要当厨师。他说自己大量使用TikTok和YouTube。“我喜欢看视频胜过看照片或消息。我看不认识的人做的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个比较害羞的人。我待在自己的泡泡里。我只看，就这样。我的反应都留在心里。”同样16岁的露西说：“我花很多时间刷内容创作者做的视频。它们比我认识的人发的帖子更有意思。”她除了偶尔发“快拍”（24小时后消失）之外，也不发帖。

无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们都已远离了社交媒体几年前还是的那种个人互动的“数字城市广场”。在法国，2026年度官方《数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“只是偶尔活跃”。在英国，Ofcom今年4月发布的一份报告显示，积极发帖的用户同比从61%降至49%。在美国，Morning Consult去年6月的一项调查发现，28%的人表示发帖频率低于前一年。现在只有33%的人每天发帖，而有57%的人每天使用社交媒体是为了娱乐。Z世代的差距更大——18%活跃发帖，74%被动浏览。瓦妮莎·拉洛是巴黎的一位临床心理学家，专攻网络行为

##段落
他表示：“用户越来越意识到，（在社交媒体上）留下的痕迹会永远存在，有些人不再想维持可能流于表面的社交媒体关系。有些人不希望承受发帖时可能招致批评的风险，也不想让自己的帖子在一堆专业内容旁边显得寒酸。”然而，拉洛补充说，人们并没有停止发帖，只是发的东西不同了，发的地方也不同了。“例如在TikTok上，年轻人发布大量内容，但更多是搞笑模仿和对现有素材的混剪再创作。目的是逗人发笑，而不是向别人讲述自己的生活。”她说，这种事仍然存在，只是从Instagram和Facebook这类社交媒体平台转移到了WhatsApp等即时通讯应用上。此外，人们也在向Instagram和Snapchat上的私密群组迁移。“这些地方私密得多，你不会被广告和网红制作的内容狂轰滥炸，”她说。“我们看到的是社交媒体正在一分为二，”社交媒体顾问、《Geekout Newsletter》作者马特·纳瓦拉说。“像Instagram和TikTok这样的大平台正变得越来越偏向娱乐和发现。WhatsApp正在成为人们真正进行社交的地方。问题在于，这类空间对企业来说更难赚钱。”小型企业主正被逼着变成主持人、编辑、趋势观察者和内容创作者，而且还是在经营业务之外——马特·纳瓦拉。正是TikTok率先开创了一种算法，从你开始滑动的那一刻就能判断你喜欢什么，然后用精心计算过的内容填满你的信息流，尽可能让你在应用上停留更久。马特·纳瓦拉说，如今“Meta已经构建了它所谓的AI系统，用于在Facebook和Instagram上推荐非关联内容，这基本上意味着，他们越来越多地向你展示你没有关注的人的内容，因为机器认为你会喜欢。它不会偏向判断：这是专业创作者吗？这是品牌吗？这是朋友吗？如果他们看到你经常与某位朋友互动，你可能会看到更多对方的内容。只是你与谁是朋友、你关注了谁，在某种程度上已经变得无关紧要了。”这一切都意味着，长期以来利用社交媒体进行免费推广的小型企业必须提升自己的水平。“对一些小型企业来说，确实存在真正的机会，”马特·纳瓦拉说。“一家面包店、花店、沙龙或本地咖啡馆，如果有一个好故事、有很强的视觉效果，或者有人们想看的幕后内容，仍然可以突围。但这也意味着工作已经变了。小型企业主正被逼着变成主持人、编辑、趋势观察者和内容创作者，而且还是在

##段落
“实际上，经营企业才是首要任务。”社交平台的主要盈利方式仍然是广告收入。这依然是核心商业模式。而且广告收入仍在持续增长——马特·纳瓦拉

##段落
社交媒体正在演变成一种类似电视的被动媒介，只不过是一台会随着你换台而自适应调整的电视。或者说，它对你了解得太透彻了，以至于它拿走了遥控器这件事似乎也没那么重要。你向平台提供关于你自己的信息，平台将其用于商业获利，作为回报，它免费为你提供量身定制、投你所好的内容。从真正的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转变，似乎确实在产生回报。“社交平台的主要盈利方式仍然是广告收入。这依然是核心商业模式。而且广告收入仍在持续增长，”马特·纳瓦拉说道。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将在2026年达到3170亿美元（2360亿英镑），高于去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）。Meta是最大的赢家。其广告销售额在2025年已经同比增长22%。今年广告销售额预计将达到2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），足以首次超越谷歌。AI驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得越来越高效和精准。“社交平台允许企业将广告植入你正在滑动浏览的内容中。每滑动三次或四次就有一条广告。而且它们是世界上最好的广告定向引擎。它们对你的兴趣了如指掌，因为你看了什么、点赞了什么、参与了什么、选择了关注什么、在应用某些板块停留了多长时间，诸如此类，”纳瓦拉说。“所以广告主会进去说：‘我想把广告投放到英国30到60岁、对DIY感兴趣的人旁边’，社交平台拥有这些信息，就会相应地投放广告。”价格取决于广告主想要的曝光量（点击量）以及定向条件的精细程度。把广告投放到买马的人的社交媒体信息流中，比投放到买冰淇淋的人的信息流中要贵。
