readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨范例，都是时间与精力、才华与爱的馈赠，并且是针对某一具体需求量身定制的。
不确定从哪里开始？以下六种时间与关注的馈赠，极有可能引发波及数百万人的连锁反应，它们来自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。
1. 转移注意力
禅宗大师一行禅师曾教导说，注意力是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨正是从这里开始——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种建立联结的行为出发，一切皆有可能。
事实是，这并不容易。我们大部分时间都迷失在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿关注他人正在面对的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。而这意味着，许多真正需要你关注的人，从未感到被我们看见。因此，注意力的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍微不舒服、放下那些盾牌、付出一些时间、冒险去关心他人的慷慨。
无论你是停下来与一个需要帮助的人建立有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经踏上了自己的慷慨之旅。
2. 搭建桥梁
在我们这个高度连接的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触那些与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在公开的网络上上演。庞大的受众会紧盯网络骂战。如果我们能为更多这类冲突带来令人满意的化解，会怎样？
主动接触批评我们的人很难。这是一种尤其具有挑战性的慷慨心态。你是在牺牲个人的舒适，以换取把人们聚在一起的更大善果。但如果你成功了，就会产生一个强大的连锁效应：你正在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。那是给我们所有人的礼物。
我们能给予的最伟大的单一礼物就是知识——解决问题的知识、满足需求的知识，或开辟前路的知话。
3. 分享知识
在无数情境中，我们能给予的最伟大的单一礼物就是知识——解决问题的知识、满足需求的知识，或开辟前路的知话。
我们给某人的最重要的一条建议

##段落
在TED舞台上演讲，意味着演讲者不应把演讲视为推销某样东西（比如一项业务或一项事业）的机会，而应把它当作一份礼物。这是一个自由地与观众分享宝贵想法的机会。而这些想法有可能在未来数年里持续影响听众的人生。

##段落
如果你拥有能让他人受益的知识，不妨想想如何将它分享出去，以产生涟漪效应。你花几个小时准备和付诸行动的事，可能点亮某个人的人生——而这或许仅仅是开始。

##段落
4. 促成连接

在我们这个高度连接的时代，我们所能触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更为重要。因此，最具感染力的慷慨行为之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立连接。最简单的方式就是做一次引荐。

##段落
正如心理学家、TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐这件事给出时相当容易——收到时却价值不可估量。问问许多人他们是如何遇见伴侣、获得梦想工作，或找到创意项目的完美合作者的，答案往往如出一辙：某个人——一位朋友、邻居、同事——把他们介绍给了对的人。你实际上做的，是让别人得以进入你的资源网络。而这些引荐可能产生指数级的连锁效应。

##段落
5. 给予款待

人类学家唐纳德·布朗在其杰出著作《人类共性》中记载，款待是被研究过的每一种文化中都观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但如果款待如此普遍（又如此令人愉悦），它真的算是一种慷慨吗？答案是肯定的。撇开任何花费不谈，邀请某人来家里——无论是朋友还是可能成为朋友的人——本身就需要付出心力。窝在沙发上看你追的剧的下一集，显然要轻松得多。

##段落
那么，款待如何能促进具有感染力的慷慨？款待触及了我们内心最深处的连接本能。而每一次被款待的体验，都会唤起一种想要回报的渴望。

##段落
人们需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健，这毋庸置疑。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑、超越——这些都是魅力的元素。

##段落
6. 创造魅力

先锋艺术家莉莉·叶曾受舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔之邀，在她家乡费城一块荒废的空地上开展一个社区艺术项目。“我很感兴趣，但完全被吓到了，”叶回忆道。“我几乎没有资源，也没有在社区环境中进行户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到一个懦夫。所以我迈出了这一步。”

##段落
这个社区项目后来成为了“艺术与人文村”，一座满是树木、雕塑和马赛克的艺术公园，由当地成年人

##与Yeh合作，为成年人和儿童创作。Yeh的作品让她深刻认识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的疗愈和变革力量。
##人们确实需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑、超越——这些都是魅力的要素。那些能够施展魅力的人，能赠予他人一份价值无可估量的礼物。

readings.title: The 'power plant' hidden inside Vermont homes
body: 20 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jack Carroll Spread across thousands of ordinary homes, this "power plant" has become Vermont's largest power source. It's protecting owners from outages and providing cheaper, cleaner energy. Vermont has faced an increase in extreme weather events in recent decades, including some of its worst storms in recorded history . For Pollyanna Bladyka, such events used to mean losing power a dozen times every year, often for multiple hours.  "I don't mind being cold… but I just want my coffee in the morning and I want to be able to watch my news," says Bladyka, who lives in the rural town of Springfield in eastern Vermont with her husband Andy and her dog. Bladyka became so fed up with the frequent power outages that in 2024 she was on the verge of buying a gas generator, as many of her neighbours had already done. But the electrician she hired to install it told her about a programme providing a compelling alternative. Run by Vermont's largest utility, Green Mountain Power (GMP), the scheme installs two batteries in participants' home for $55 (£41) a month over a 10-year lease agreement . After doing some research, Bladyka and her husband decided it was a better option than the $12,000 (£9,000) cost of the generator they had planned to buy. They have not lost power a single time since the system was installed in 2024. I'd like to say I did it for the environment, but I did it for myself. But I don't mind helping – Pollyanna Bladyka More than 5,500 people in Vermont have similar home battery systems. As well as providing individual homes energy security during power outages, these batteries form the backbone of a new kind of system known as a virtual power plant that mimics the resources of a traditional power plant. The US now has over 40GW of virtual power plant capacity, according to internal analysis by Wood Mackenzie. It's still relatively small compared to the roughly 600GW of natural gas and 200GW of coal , but a total of 160GW of capacity could be unlocked by 2030 , according to a 2025 US Department of Energy report – equal to some 20% of the country's expected peak energy demand. Through GMP's programme, its virtual power plant has quietly become Vermont's biggest source of power. Now, the state is testing how far this "hidden" form of power can go.    For Bladyka, avoiding outages was the main reason she got the battery. "I'd like to say I did it for the environment, but I did it for myself," she tells me on a visit to her home in May 2026. "But I don't mind helping." She describes previously waking up without power multiple times per year and not being able to go about her morning routine, with storms the most frequent cause, she says. Virtual power plants can give a huge advantage over traditional systems when it comes to resilience against power outages. Rise of the virtual plant Virtual power plants are an aggregation of thousands (or even millions) of consumer devices into one orchestrated system that fits into the wider grid like a traditional power plant. Everything from home batteries and rooftop solar to smart thermostats and even EV batteries can be incorporated. This system is coordinated to reduce demand on the grid – replacing the need to build extra fossil fuel-powered plants.  The concept has been around for decades , but has gained popularity in recent years as energy demand has risen and more distributed energy resources like rooftop solar have been added to the grid. Virtual power plants are now being built everywhere from Germany to China . Climate change is driving an increase in extreme weather globally and Vermont has seen that trend firsthand, from flooding to snowstorms . It may not come as a surprise then that the state has experienced an increase in outages in recent decades (as has the US as a whole), according to a 2022 Associated Press analysis of government data. In fact, seven of the 10 most damaging storms in GMP's history have happened in the last decade, the company tells the BBC, causing more than $225m (£168m) in damages . Given the state's rural nature and extreme cold in the winter, any kind of prolonged outage can be a matter of life-and-death if a customer does not have backup power – as it was during Texas' grid failure in 2021.  Now, though, power cuts are not a worry, says Bladyka – her battery should be able to power her house for two days, so long as electricity usage on things like dishwashing and laundry is kept to a minimum. Megan Browning, who lives in northern Vermont with her family, has had two home batteries through the GMP programme as well as rooftop solar for around a year and has not lost power since. When a recent severe windstorm knocked down a power line near her home, she says, many houses in her neighbourhood lost power, but she "didn't even notice a flicker".  Others in Vermont have likewise decided that enough is enough when it comes to outages. GMP saw a surge of enrolments in the battery lease programme in 2023, when state regulators lifted a cap on it. Enrolment has continued to grow steadily ever since, it adds, with over 2,500 people enrolled since 2023. GMP, which serves over 75% of Vermont, has a goal of eliminating all power outages by 2030 . The battery programme plays a strong role in its plan, alongside other measures like undergrounding power lines. In fact, in some rural and more outage-prone areas, GMP sees home energy storage as so important to its goal of preventing outages that it has proposed giving thousands of customers batteries at no cost. It has already done so on a small scale through multiple pilot projects . Several virtual power plants have emerged in the US in recent years as people catch on to their promise, says Kate Peters, a virtual power plant expert at Boston-based consultancy The Brattle Group.  But GMP's programme, which began as a pilot in 2017, may be one of the largest battery programmes in the US, says Peters. The company can tap into Bladyka's batteries (and everyone else in the programme's) whenever needed, though the customer always retains some reserve power for themselves, especially during outages. It links these batteries in with an array of other resources including EV batteries, commercial demand response and a handful of utility-scale batteries.    The programme now provides some 110MW of power –  about the same as a small-to-average-sized natural gas plant – and is the largest power source in the state. Virtual power plants themselves don't actually produce power, though the solar panels tapped into it do (around 50% of the houses in its programme with home batteries also have solar panels, GMP says). Instead, they use software to manage and conserve energy in more intelligent ways, making what we have already go further – especially at the times the grid needs it the most.  Many experts now view such systems as a power plant – and by extension electric grid – of the future. They are innovative, resilient and more efficient than the traditional way utilities have supplied power, says Mari McClure, the chief executive of GMP.  "We believe in a two-way grid," she told me on a visit to the company's headquarters in May 2026. "With technology nowadays, we can create a distributed, decentralised model that's much more affordable and much safer. Customers really become consumers and producers."   The grid in Vermont, as well as most places in the US, was built to meet peak demand – the time when electricity use is at its highest. In many places, however, that peak is often only seen on a handful of days per year .  Utilities conventionally build entire power plants, known as "peaker plants", just to serve this purpose. Run on fossil fuels, they are often both expensive and highly polluting . GMP similarly used to rely on oil, diesel and natural gas peaker plants to meet peak demand. Now the company's virtual power plant has effectively replaced them, says McClure. "We've been slowly able to decommission those as they've become end-of-life," she says. (Four peaking plants still run very occasionally if the regional New England grid operator calls on them, GMP says, though it hopes to close them all soon.) Rocky Mountain Power in Utah is another utility that has effectively replaced peaker plants with home batteries , albeit on a smaller scale. In fact, research has found that virtual power plants could fill the role that peaker plants have played across the US – and often at a much lower cost, which would likely lower customers' bills . "A virtual power plant is a way for a utility to pay people to provide some of the services that they usually pay big companies to provide for the grid," says Ben Hertz-Shargel, president of the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities and an expert on distributed energy sources. Besides outage prevention, this lower cost is arguably the biggest benefit to customers. GMP's virtual power plant saved customers $11m (£8m) last year, the company told the BBC. The US Department of Energy found these plants could save the US over $10bn (£7.4bn) annually by 2030 .  "When we look at what's the most impactful thing we can do to really maximise the grid and take it to the next level, the answer [always] comes back to virtual power plants," says McClure. Virtual power plants still face barriers in the US. The most significant is a "backwards financial incentive structure" that dissuades utilities from using them, says Jen Downing, a former US Department of Energy official and lead author of its 2023 virtual power plant report .   "Utilities don't have much incentive to harness demand flexibility because they make more money if they just build stuff," she says. "That's probably the number one issue nationally," she adds, though noting it's not the case for every utility. Other hindrances can include the cost of enrolling customers into programmes in the first place and difficulties integrating virtual power plants into wholesale electricity markets .   The tide may finally be turning in the US, however, according to Downing, with states like Massachusetts , Illinois and New Jersey pushing utilities to procure capacity from virtual power plants in an effort to bring down energy costs.  States and tech companies are now also looking to them as a way to make room on the grid for data centres. More like this: •  Seoul has solved a New York food waste problem •  The Pacific warming patterns warping US weather •  The 'wonder material' that could transform solar In the coming years, GMP aims to offer all its almost 300,000 customers energy storage if they want it, says McClure, with ambitions to more than double the size of its virtual power plant by 2034. It also hopes to expand its resource base , plugging in the thousands of EV batteries in Vermont, for example, to provide a significant distributed resource – a concept known as "vehicle-to-grid". Since the storage capacity of EV batteries is so large, this could be a potential gamechanger for virtual power plants everywhere. It remains to be seen whether that will happen, though, says Downing. "If you look at the total storage capacity of EV batteries, it's enormous, but I don't think it's really cost-effective today for most consumer EVs," she says.   McClure has experienced its potential first hand: during one outage, she powered her rural home for five days with the battery from her electric Ford F-150 Lightning truck, she says. Whichever technologies end up powering virtual power plants, they're likely to involve local communities more than traditional energy systems have, says Hertz-Shargel. People working in large groups, he says, can be "as big as a power plant". -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the Future Earth newsletter, while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week. ##段落
20小时前 分享 保存 在Google上添加为首选 Jack Carroll 分散在数千个普通家庭中，这座"发电厂"已成为佛蒙特州最大的电力来源。它为业主提供停电保护，并带来更便宜、更清洁的能源。近几十年来，佛蒙特州经历了越来越多的极端天气事件，其中包括有记录以来最严重的几场风暴。对于Pollyanna Bladyka来说，这类事件过去意味着每年停电十几次，而且常常持续数小时。

##段落
"我不介意挨冻……但我早上就是想要喝上咖啡，还想能看看新闻，"Bladyka说。她与丈夫Andy以及爱犬住在佛蒙特州东部乡村小镇斯普林菲尔德。Bladyka对频繁停电实在忍无可忍，以至于在2024年，她差点就要买一台燃气发电机，就像她许多邻居已经做的那样。但她雇来安装发电机的电工告诉她，有一个项目提供了颇具吸引力的替代方案。

##段落
该计划由佛蒙特州最大的公用事业公司Green Mountain Power（GMP）运营，根据一份为期10年的租赁协议，以每月55美元（41英镑）的价格在参与者家中安装两块电池。在做了一些研究后，Bladyka和丈夫认为，这比他们原本打算购买、价值12,000美元（9,000英镑）的发电机更划算。自2024年该系统安装以来，他们家一次电也没停过。我想说我是为了环境才这么做的，但我是为了自己。不过我也不介意帮上忙——Pollyanna Bladyka

##段落
佛蒙特州有超过5,500人拥有类似的家庭电池系统。这些电池不仅能在停电期间为单个家庭提供能源保障，还构成了一种被称为虚拟电厂的新型系统的骨干，这种系统模仿传统发电厂的资源。根据Wood Mackenzie的内部分析，美国目前拥有超过40GW的虚拟电厂容量。与大约600GW的天然气和200GW的煤炭相比，这仍然相对较小，但根据美国能源部2025年的一份报告，到2030年总共可释放160GW的容量——相当于美国预计峰值能源需求的约20%。

##段落
通过GMP的项目，其虚拟电厂已悄然成为佛蒙特州最大的电力来源。如今，该州正在测试这种"隐藏"形式的电力还能走多远。对Bladyka来说，避免停电是她购买电池的主要原因。"我想说我是为了环境才这么做的，但我是为了自己，"她在2026年5月我拜访她家时告诉我。"不过我也不介意帮上忙。"她说，以前自己每年都会多次在停电中醒来，无法进行早晨的日常安排，而风暴是最常见的原因。虚拟电厂相较传统

##段落
在应对停电的韧性方面，人工智能系统也是如此。

##段落
虚拟电厂的崛起。虚拟电厂将成千上万（甚至数百万）的消费者设备聚合为一个协调统一的系统，像传统电厂一样接入更广泛的电网。从家用电池和屋顶太阳能，到智能恒温器甚至电动汽车电池，都可以被纳入其中。该系统经过协调调度以降低电网需求——从而替代了增建化石燃料电厂的需要。这一概念已存在数十年，但近年来随着能源需求上升以及屋顶太阳能等更多分布式能源资源接入电网，它重新获得了广泛关注。如今，从德国到中国，虚拟电厂正在各地兴建。气候变化正在推动全球极端天气的增加，佛蒙特州亲身经历了这一趋势——从洪水到暴风雪。因此，根据美联社2022年对政府数据的分析，该州近几十年来停电次数有所增加（全美整体也是如此），这或许并不令人意外。事实上，GMP公司告诉BBC，该公司历史上破坏最严重的10场风暴中有7场发生在过去十年，造成了超过2.25亿美元（1.68亿英镑）的损失。鉴于该州的乡村性质和冬季极端寒冷，任何形式的长时间停电都可能关乎生死——如果客户没有备用电源的话——正如2021年德克萨斯州电网崩溃期间的情况一样。不过，布拉迪卡说，现在停电已不再是困扰——她的电池应该能够为房屋供电两天，只要洗碗和洗衣等用电保持在最低水平。梅根·布朗宁与家人住在佛蒙特州北部，她通过GMP项目安装了两块家用电池以及屋顶太阳能，大约一年以来从未断电。她说，当最近一场严重的风暴刮倒了她家附近的一条电线时，她所在社区的许多房屋都停了电，但她“连一次闪烁都没察觉到”。佛蒙特州的其他居民同样认为，在停电问题上，忍无可忍无需再忍。GMP在2023年看到电池租赁项目的报名人数激增，当时州监管机构取消了该项目的人数上限。该公司补充说，自那以后报名人数持续稳步增长，自2023年以来已有超过2500人报名。GMP为佛蒙特州超过75%的区域供电，其目标是到2030年消除所有停电。电池项目在其计划中发挥着重要作用，与地下电缆等其他措施并列。事实上，在一些乡村和更容易停电的地区，GMP认为家庭储能对实现防止停电的目标至关重要，以至于它提议免费向数千名客户提供电池。它已经这样做了。

##段落
在美国，近年来随着人们逐渐认识到虚拟电厂的潜力，已涌现出多个虚拟电厂项目，但规模都较小。波士顿咨询公司The Brattle Group的虚拟电厂专家凯特·彼得斯表示，GMP的项目始于2017年的试点，可能是美国最大的电池项目之一。该公司可以在需要时接入布拉迪卡的电池（以及项目中其他所有人的电池），不过客户始终保留一部分备用电力，尤其是在停电期间。它将这些电池与一系列其他资源连接起来，包括电动汽车电池、商业需求响应和少数公用事业规模电池。

##段落
该项目目前提供约110兆瓦的电力——大约相当于一座中小型天然气发电厂——是该州最大的电力来源。虚拟电厂本身并不实际发电，尽管接入其中的太阳能板确实在发电（GMP表示，该项目中约50%装有家用电池的房屋也装有太阳能板）。相反，它们使用软件以更智能的方式管理和节约能源，让我们已有的资源发挥更大作用——尤其是在电网最需要的时候。

##段落
许多专家现在将此类系统视为未来的发电厂——进而也是未来的电网。GMP首席执行官玛丽·麦克卢尔表示，它们具有创新性、韧性，并且比公用事业公司传统的供电方式更高效。

##段落
“我们相信双向电网，”她在2026年5月访问该公司总部时告诉我。“有了当今的技术，我们可以创建一个分布式、去中心化的模式，更加经济实惠，也更加安全。客户真正成为了消费者和生产者的结合体。”

##段落
佛蒙特州的电网，以及美国大多数地方的电网，都是为了满足峰值需求——即用电量最高的时段——而建设的。然而在许多地方，这种峰值往往每年只出现几天。公用事业公司通常专门建造整座发电厂，即所谓的“调峰电厂”，仅仅为了满足这一需求。这些电厂以化石燃料为动力，往往既昂贵又污染严重。GMP过去也同样依赖燃油、柴油和天然气调峰电厂来满足峰值需求。麦克卢尔表示，现在该公司的虚拟电厂已经有效取代了它们。“随着这些电厂寿命终结，我们一直在逐步将其退役，”她说。（GMP表示，如果新英格兰地区电网运营商调用，仍有四座调峰电厂会偶尔运行，但公司希望尽快将它们全部关闭。）犹他州的落基山电力公司是另一家以家用电池有效取代调峰电厂的公用事业公司，尽管规模较小。事实上，研究发现，虚拟……

##段落
虚拟电厂可以填补美国各地调峰电厂所扮演的角色——而且成本往往低得多，这很可能会降低用户的电费账单。“虚拟电厂是一种让公用事业公司付费给民众、让他们提供一些原本要花大价钱请大公司为电网提供的服务的方式，”新泽西州公共事业委员会主席、分布式能源专家本·赫茨-沙格尔说。除了防止停电之外，这种更低的成本可以说是对用户最大的好处。GMP公司告诉BBC，其虚拟电厂去年为用户节省了1100万美元（800万英镑）。美国能源部发现，到2030年，这类电厂每年可为美国节省超过100亿美元（74亿英镑）。“当我们审视自己能做的最有影响力的事情是什么，以真正最大化电网效能、将其提升到新的水平时，答案（总是）回到虚拟电厂，”麦克卢尔说。虚拟电厂在美国仍然面临障碍。最突出的问题是“逆向的财务激励结构”，它使公用事业公司不愿采用虚拟电厂，美国能源部前官员、其2023年虚拟电厂报告的主要作者珍·唐宁说。“公用事业公司没有多少动力去利用需求灵活性，因为它们只要建设设施就能赚更多钱，”她说。“这可能是全国范围内的头号问题，”她补充道，不过她也指出并非每家公用事业公司都是如此。其他障碍可能包括最初让用户加入项目的成本，以及将虚拟电厂整合进批发电力市场的困难。不过，据唐宁所说，美国的风向可能终于要转变了，马萨诸塞州、伊利诺伊州和新泽西州等州正在推动公用事业公司从虚拟电厂采购容量，以降低能源成本。各州和科技公司现在也把它们视为在电网上为数据中心腾出空间的一种方式。更多类似内容：• 首尔解决了纽约的食品浪费问题 • 正在扭曲美国天气的太平洋变暖模式 • 可能改变太阳能格局的“神奇材料”。麦克卢尔说，未来几年，GMP计划为几乎所有近30万用户提供储能服务，只要他们愿意，并立志到2034年将其虚拟电厂的规模扩大一倍以上。它还希望扩大其资源基础，例如接入佛蒙特州数千块电动汽车电池，以提供可观的分布式资源——这一概念被称为“车网互动”。由于电动汽车电池的储能容量如此之大，这可能成为各地虚拟电厂的潜在游戏规则改变者。不过，唐宁说，这是否会实现仍有待观察。“如果你看看电动汽车电池的总储能容量，那是巨大

## 她表示：“对我们来说是这样，但我并不认为如今对大多数消费级电动汽车而言，这真的具有成本效益。”麦克卢尔亲身感受到了这项技术的潜力：她说，在一次停电期间，她用自己的福特F-150 Lightning电动皮卡的电池为位于乡村的家供电长达五天。赫兹-沙格尔表示，无论最终是哪些技术为虚拟电厂提供电力，它们都可能比传统能源系统更多地涉及当地社区。他说，以大规模群体方式协作的人们，其作用可以“像一座发电厂一样大”。——欲获取重要气候新闻和充满希望的进展，请订阅《未来地球》简报；《必读清单》则每周两次为你精选特写与洞见。欲了解更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。地球 气候变化 可再生能源 太阳能 未来星球 特写

readings.title: Trump’s China reversal
body: Today, Explained newsletter Trump’s China reversal The president made confrontation with China core to his political identity. Now he’s walking it back. by Caitlin Dewey Sep 28, 2026, 8:44 PM UTC Gift President Donald Trump shakes hands with China’s President Xi Jinping on September 25, 2026. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . I have good news and bad news for the holiday shoppers in the audience. The good news is that the US and China announced this morning — in the wake of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s three-day visit to DC — that the two countries are suspending tariffs on $60 billion of goods , including Christmas ornaments, toys and other tchotchkes. The bad news is that, because retailers ship goods for the winter holidays well in advance, these reductions might come a bit too late to affect this year’s bills. But there’s always 2027, right? Barring another unforeseen trade altercation. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. The tariff rollback represents a real and continued de-escalation in the trade war between China and the US, which — at one point last year — was slapping Chinese goods with a whopping 145 percent tariff . But it’s not a conclusive truce, either. The new agreement doesn’t address the touchiest products for either country, like rare earth minerals (which are used in electronics and clean energy tech) and advanced chips (which are critical to AI development). China also didn’t lower its tariffs on soybeans, which have hit some American farmers so hard they’re thinking of voting for Democrats . There’s a certain irony to President Donald Trump’s about-face on the Chinese tariffs, incomplete though it may be. For years, the president made confrontation with China central to his political identity and reaped the benefits in votes. Now he appears to be circling back to what was, for decades, the mainstream, default Republican position: Namely, that more and freer trade with China is ultimately good for American consumers and businesses. President Richard Nixon first set that tone 54 years ago, when he famously became the first US president to visit Beijing. Subsequent GOP leaders leaned further into free trade with China, even as they railed against the evils of communism. Greater trade will bring “great benefits…to all our peoples,” George W. Bush said in a 2001 statement celebrating China’s entry into the World Trade Organization. But those “great benefits” were a mixed bag for some Americans, history suggests. The price of US consumer goods did fall in the early 2000s as trade between the US and China exploded. At the same time, US manufacturing towns suffered job losses so severe and concentrated that some still haven’t recovered. Those job losses may have helped propel Trump to the White House , at least in his first term. Researchers have found that communities hit hardest by Chinese competition elected more extreme Congressional candidates in 2010, and then swung hardest to Trump in the 2016 election. One 2016 paper by a highly regarded team of economists actually calculated that — in an alternate reality where US-China trade grew half as quickly between 2001 and 2016 — Hillary Clinton would have won North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Michigan...and thus, the presidency. In other words, Trump tapped into real harms and anxieties when he veered from the GOP’s usual stance on China 10 years ago. And he might be attempting to address new economic anxieties about inflation and living costs by reversing his course on China again now. Call it Trump’s Nixon-to-China moment. The question, of course, is whether voters will give Trump credit for (partially) solving a problem that he himself created. ➨ “Microdose” movement. As the weather gradually and inexorably gets colder, many of us will see our daily step counts fall off. You could do as the Swedes do and load up on layers… or you could stay safely indoors and try microdosing movement . Just five minutes every half hour can help reduce the health impacts of extended sitting. Try tying little walks to a specific cue, like the need to refill your water bottle or the end of a meeting. Did you know… that scientists believe roughly 90 percent of species on Earth still haven’t been identified or discovered ? These unknown species are generally unglamorous: Think insects, mites, and crustaceans. Today’s trivia: What is the name of Quasimodo’s (unrequited) love interest in Victor Hugo’s classic novel The Hunchback of Notre Dame ? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the film that won Best Picture at the 85th Academy Awards. That would be Argo , a political thriller about the 1979 Iran hostage crisis. ##历史表明，这些“巨大好处”对一些美国人来说喜忧参半。21世纪初，随着美中贸易迅猛发展，美国消费品价格确实下降了。与此同时，美国制造业城镇遭受的失业如此严重且集中，以至于一些地方至今仍未恢复。这些失业可能助推了特朗普入主白宫，至少在他的第一个任期内是如此。研究人员发现，受中国竞争冲击最严重的社区在2010年选出了更极端的国会候选人，随后在2016年大选中又最猛烈地倒向特朗普。2016年一篇由备受尊敬的经济学家团队撰写的论文实际上计算出——在一个反事实情境中，如果2001年至2016年间美中贸易增速只有实际的一半——希拉里·克林顿本会赢得北卡罗来纳、宾夕法尼亚、威斯康星和密歇根……从而赢得总统职位。换句话说，特朗普10年前偏离共和党对华常规立场时，触及的是真实的伤害与焦虑。而他现在可能正试图通过再次逆转对华路线，来回应围绕通胀和生活成本的新经济焦虑。不妨称之为特朗普的“尼克松访华时刻”。当然，问题在于选民是否会认可特朗普（部分）解决了一个他自己制造的问题。

##“微量运动”风潮。随着天气逐渐且不可阻挡地变冷，我们许多人的每日步数都会下降。你可以像瑞典人那样层层叠穿……或者你也可以安全地待在室内，尝试“微量运动”。每半小时只需五分钟，就有助于减轻久坐对健康的影响。试着把短距离走动绑定到某个具体提示上，比如需要续水或会议结束时。你知道吗……科学家认为地球上大约90%的物种仍未被识别或发现？这些未知物种通常并不起眼：想想昆虫、螨虫和甲壳类动物。今日小知识：在维克多·雨果的经典小说《巴黎圣母院》中，卡西莫多（无果）爱慕的对象叫什么名字？（你可以在Vox每日填字游戏中找到这个以及其他脑力谜题。答案见明日版。）昨日小知识：上周我们问你，第85届奥斯卡金像奖最佳影片得主是哪部电影。答案是《逃离德黑兰》，一部关于1979年伊朗人质危机的政治惊悚片。查看更多：中国政治 今日解析通讯 世界政治 大型石油公司向最高法院提出了一项大胆请求 用最新的Vox填字游戏让大脑休息一下 一个天坑吞没了尼古拉斯·凯奇的私人车道。你的可能下一个就是。美国空置的卧室正待争夺 Flock摄像头令人不安。它们可能仍然值得使用。邮箱（必填） 注册 提交你的邮箱，即表示你同意我们的条款和

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.

##段落
前宇航员分享的3个高效领导力策略
2023年12月4日
/
约瑟夫·德布林
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
Reddit
WhatsApp
玛丽亚·佩特里希娜 / iStock
“ data-large-file=”https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770“ /> 玛丽亚·佩特里希娜 / iStock
领导力究竟是什么样的？
虽然带领团队有各种不同的方式，但在寻找高效领导风格的过程中，我们许多人都会遇到一些共同的问题：我怎样才能为团队提供支持？我需要让人敬畏，还是要赢得尊重？而最关键的问题是：我怎样才能确保团队信任我？
凯迪·科尔曼在她的职业生涯中——作为化学家、工程师、空军上校和宇航员——一直在面对这些问题。在与TED科学策展人大卫·别洛的对话中，科尔曼分享了三个建立并维持领导者信任的策略。无论你从事什么职业，这些建议都能帮助你让团队做好准备，去面对任何挑战——无论是在外太空还是在地球上。
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有。
1. 勇于把团队成员当作独立的个体来了解
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但科尔曼认为，也许应该有。你团队中的每个成员都是一个完整的人，而且由于我们在工作中面临的许多问题都是跨学科的，了解每个人在朝九晚五之外是什么样的人非常有价值。愿意以这种脆弱的方式去了解你的团队，是任何领导者必备的核心技能。
科尔曼说，当你能说出“我觉得你的世界和我的不同，我想更多地了解它”时，你不仅在建立信任，还在打开一条沟通渠道，让你更深入地了解队友的特质。这类对话需要你愿意并勇于展现脆弱。一旦你了解了每个人能带来什么，你就能促进那些能带领团队走向共同成功的品质不断成长。
例如，当科尔曼为空间站生活做准备时，她的顾问们警告说，长时间远离家人可能让人难以承受。然而对她来说，这并不是问题——她已经通勤并在远离家人的情况下工作了十多年。在分享了自己的经历后，她的同事们意识到，她不仅能适应空间站的生活，还能帮助其他人应对这种变化。
2. 创造一种对所有人想法都开放的文化
虽然领导者必须引导团队，但同样重要的是让每个人都知道，他们可以为自己发声，并把自己的想法摆到桌面上。
科尔曼在美国宇航局接受太空训练时，就受益于这样的领导方式

##段落
在预算削减的情况下，NASA宣布将取消较小尺寸的宇航服，这意味着如果某人没有资格使用较大尺寸的宇航服，就无法前往空间站。这给科尔曼带来了一个选择：等待NASA采购适合她的宇航服，或者想办法穿着较大尺寸的宇航服进行训练。通过与NASA的决策者合作，科尔曼得以将训练转为使用较大的宇航服。她说，如果她没有感到可以自由发声，她可能还要再等10年才能穿着小号宇航服前往空间站。

##段落
当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其余的事情就会更容易各就各位。

##段落
3. 把信任作为你的使命

有时候，在工作场所建立信任可能比你预想的更困难，但当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其余的事情就会更容易各就各位。职场动态始终在变化——也许某位队友的工作/生活优先级发生了变化，或者一个重大失误要求你们所有人都在新的压力下协同工作。这些挑战使培养信任变得棘手，但它们同样是机会时刻。

##段落
如果出现了新的挑战，或者信任已被破坏，科尔曼提醒我们要“始终弄清楚原因和内容”。务必问一问：为什么会发生这件事，他们为什么会有这种感受，以及对此能做些什么？对不同观点保持开放，如果一开始没有沟通成功，也不要放弃。联结往往存在于你所做的更小的事情中；聊聊食物或音乐，写一张便条称赞某个想法，并请对方多说一些。这种程度的联结和脆弱感一开始可能并不直观，但当你把信任作为使命的核心部分时，它就会变得容易。

##段落
科尔曼提醒我们，信任既是给予的，也是赢得的。作为一名女性，她知道赢得某些男性同事的信任可能格外具有挑战性。她的方法很简单：她表现出色，并以耐心和坚持学习同事的语言，也教他们理解她的语言。赢得信任的挑战永远都会存在，但如果你为团队示范脆弱、开放和理解，你会发现回报也永远都会存在。
